speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
maintopic: MOTIONS UNDER S.O. 43   HUMAN RIGHTS SOVIET AUTHORITIES URGED TO FREE ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The harassment and imprisonment of Anatoly Shcharansky have been the subject of previous emergency motions in this House. Mr. Shcharansky, a leading Soviet refusenik and internationally renowned scholar, has been on a hunger strike for several weeks, as a means to obtaining his freedom. His rapidly deteriorating health now places his life in very grave danger. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley):
That this House urge Soviet authorities to immediately grant Anatoly Shcharansky the freedom for which he is so valiantly struggling, thus ending his hunger strike and the grave threat to his life. The Soviet authorities should do this, both for humanitarian reasons, and in accordance with the terms of the Helsinki Final Act.

Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Since there is one acre of agricultural land for every citizen on earth, and whereas we in Canada enjoy the luxury of three acres of agricultural land for every Canadian, but because we are destroying our food producing lands at a rate whereby we will be left with only three-quarters of an acre of farm land per Canadian citizen by the year 2005, and since Canada has no co-ordinated effort toward preservation of agricultural lands, I move, seconded by the Hon. That this Parliament encourage the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of the Environment to cause appropriate consultation with provincial governments and Canadian soil scientists, bearing in mind the provincial nature of this issue, and seek their co-operation to establish an umbrella agency whose objective is to preserve and improve agricultural lands in Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity occasioned by the news in the media that over 600 refugees in Canada, many of them from El Salvador, have recently been cut off from receiving any public assistance. This underlines the fact that the Government normally takes a year or a year and a half to process their applications. Very many of them have been refused effective permission to work to maintain themselves and their families, and the Government has failed to acquaint its own staff fully with special provisions for Salvadoran refugees. Therefore I move seconded by the Hon. Member for Cowi-chan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly):
That the Government instruct all of its staff fully on the special provisions for Salvadoran refugees, give them temporary permission to work while they await the Government's decision on their fate, and add the necessary staff to the Refugee Status Advisory Committee to speed up the processing beyond the present timing of a year and a half.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Quietly, subtly, inch by inch, the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada and his Liberal hierarchy are
getting control of every segment of Canadian life: through NEP and Bill C-48, energy; through the CRTC, telecommunications; through the taxpayers money, the arts; through Canagrex, the food industry; through bills like Bill C-137, the workers; through definition of a letter, the mail; and on it goes. That this House urges every organization and all individuals in Canada who value their freedom and their liberties to rise up and demand the resignation of this dictatorial Government.

Madam Speaker, I rise, pursuant to Standing Order 43, to speak on a matter of continuing concern. The abysmal record of the Soviet regime in respect of basic human rights, as per the United Nations Charter and the 1975 Helsinki Accords, continues unabated. The world demands and expects nations to respect the conventions of documents they have signed; deeds, not words, are the hallmark of international trust, justice and fair play.
Given the imprisonment or forced emigration of virtually all members of the Helsinki Watch Group in the Soviet Union, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) and the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie):
That this House condemn the continued abuse of human rights and violations of the Helsinki Final Act in the Soviet Union in contravention of recognized international obligation.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct my questions to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs as a follow-up to questions directed by my Leader yesterday to the same Minister. The Minister will recall that in yesterday's exchange he was asked why Bill S-31 was presented to the Senate and not to the House of Commons, and whether that matter could be discussed.
In view of the consternation the Bill is creating among the people whom it will directly affect, namely, the people of the provinces of Canada, I would like to ask the Minister whether there was any consultation with regard to the nature and spirit of Bill S-31 prior to its presentation in the Senate. Additionally, in view of the consternation which has developed with regard to Bill S-31, could he tell us whether he has held any consultation with the provinces subsequent to the time it was introduced in the Senate, and whether he could report on such consultation, if it took place?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not know what consternation the Hon. Member is referring to. In fact, 1 believe this bill has been well received by all business circles across Canada. I also think that has been the case among the provinces, which clearly recognize the primacy of the Canadian Government in the transportation sector covered in this bill.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not think the Minister would really want to follow up by saying that it was well received by business, or that he would want to leave the impression that the provinces are in agreement with Bill S-31, nor is anyone arguing about primacy. What a person is arguing about here concerns the co-operative federalism which the Prime Minister once declared dead and tried to resurrect two weeks ago, and which now the Minister, by his actions, is saying is of little consequence in practical terms for the Government. That is the issue.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I would like to ask the same Minister a supplementary question with regard to the legislation which goes into the transportation aspects and what he calls the federal primacy, and no one is arguing that point. For example, hydroelectric lines are not directly mentioned in the Bill and are not dealt with as being pipelines. However, the Minister has referred to Part III of the National Energy Act which in fact includes hydroelectric lines. Are hydro lines included under the provisions of the Bill? Are hydro lines
which are to be used for the purpose of exporting electrical energy to another country, included in the Bill as they are in Part III of the National Energy Act?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I may remind the hon. member that our reasons for introducing this legislation were to prevent any future conflicts with the provinces. We thought it was vital to act now, in order to prevent any erroneous interpretations or being obliged to correct situations that might arise later on. To my knowledge, we have had no reactions to the bill, except for one from a minister. Only one provincial minister has commented to date on the bill and that was the Minister of Transport from Quebec. I do not know whether the hon. member has received instructions from the Parti Quebecois to ask questions in the House today, but as far as I know, that is the only government that has reacted to the bill until now.
We do not want any fights with the provinces. That is certainly not our intent. The bill clearly establishes the rules for the future and safeguards the primacy of the federal government in this area in clear and carefully defined terms. The hon. member asked a specific question regarding power transmission lines. I may point out that if he reads the bill carefully, he will find that these lines are not affected by the bill. If he wants us to add an amendment, this will be considered at the appropriate time.

Madam Speaker, I should like to put a supplementary question to the Minister, whose defence is personal attack. He can do that, but if it is the level to which he has to resort, it is, of course, just the voice of the desperate. We will leave it at that.
The Minister says he wants no fight with the provinces and that he wants to avoid any future difficulty. He knows that the legislation can be made retroactive through court action, however. The Minister knows that, so what is he trying to prevent? He says it is not directed at the provinces, but it is, whether one wants to talk about Northlands Rail, about B.C. Rail, or about the transportation system in the potash industry-the list goes on and on.
When will the Minister sit down with the provinces to look at these specific issues, if he says he does not want any fight and wants co-operative federalism? He knows very well that what he has embarked upon is the very fight that he claims to want to prevent.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
that Bill C-134, respecting rebates of interest on farm loans made under the Farm Credit Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Madam Speaker, Bill C-134 is an Act respecting rebate of interest on farm loans made under the Farm Credit Act and is a piece of legislation which is extremely important to the farm community and to all Canadians.
Hon. Members will recall that in the June 28, 1982 budget speech, the then Minister of Finance announced a special loans program to assist farmers in financial distress. Contrary to what some Members say here, the Minister had a program that was quite significant and farmers who have benefited from it think it is quite significant. Under the special Farm Financial Assistance Program, the then Minister of Finance had allocated a total of $100 million for loans in fiscal years
1982-	1983 and 1983-1984 and for interest rebates on these loans for a total of $200 million. Because of the pressing demand for assistance this year, this allocation has now changed to $130 million for 1982-1983 and $70 million for
1983-	1984.
The funding from the then Minister of Finance, combined with that from other FCC sources, will result in loan approvals of $200 million, on which a subsidy of four percentage points will be paid for two years. This measure will help to assure the survival of many Canadian farmers who are presently facing serious financial difficulties. The Farm Credit Corporation credit advisers will assist farmers in the development of farm plans which will provide for greater financial stability at the end of the two-year rebate program.
The Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act is required in order to provide the statutory authority for the appropriation of an amount of $16 million, not zero but $16 million, for the payment of the interest rebate of four percentage points of the principal amount of farm loans made under this special program.
The Farm Credit Act does not provide the Farm Credit Corporation with the authority to rebate any portion of the interest charged under the Act, nor is there other appropriation legislation through which the subsidy could be paid. Thus, after a review of all other options, the proposed legislation was deemed to be the most acceptable method by which to pay the subsidy.
Under the special Farm Financial Assistance Program, loans will be made at the regular Farm Credit lending rate which on June 29, 1982 was 16.5 per cent and on October 1, 1982 was set at 15 and % per cent. The rebate of four percentage points over two years to date reduces the farmers' effective interest rate cost to 11 and % per cent. FCC customary lending criteria will apply. For example, a loan ceiling of $300,000 for individuals and $500,000 for more than one qualifying applicant will apply and a maximum amortization period of up to 30 years is still in effect.
This is what most Members must keep in mind. No one is willing to loan long-term money now, at least hardly anyone we could find. We were offered some Canadian money for up to 10 years, I believe it was around $50 million, with an interest rate of 14 per cent. We refused that because we are confident that interest rates will go down even further and we will be able to obtain long-term money, using the agribond principle that was not originally thought up by those opposite, Mr. Speaker, but was thought up and talked about by people for many years, probably even before the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) thought of coming to the House of Commons. I can remember when it was first thought of and talked about by farm organizations and politicians several years ago.
We must still have long-term money in agriculture. At the present time, the demand for money is not as great as it was at one time because there are not as many farm transfers taking place in 1982. Any farmer in financial distress may apply for this special loan under this Program. The farmer is required to prepare an acceptable plan of recovery in consultation with the Farm Credit Corporation. In addition, he or she must demonstrate that the farm operation will be able to generate sufficient income after two years to meet anticipated commitments.
From the time the special Program was announced on June 28, 1982, up to October 26, 1982, 554 loans had been approved, totalling $80.1 million. Including applications in process, the total loan commitment to October 26, 1982, under this special Program is estimated at $105 million, which indicates the demand from farmers in financial distress for these special loans. This is contrary to the figures that the
November 4, 1982

Hon. Member used when quoting, I believe, from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We say that with that Program we will probably help approximately 2,000 farmers.
When we break down the numbers of those who received loans into regions, it is interesting to see where those farmers are. The number of farmers in British Columbia who received these loans was 23. The amount of the loans was $5.3 million.
I am surprised that there would be farmers in Alberta applying for a Farm Credit Corporation loan.
Mir. Paproski: Why?

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
I thought they had many different programs there. They have about five different programs in Alberta that provide funds for farmers. Most of the other Provinces cannot even afford to have one of those programs. There were 42 farmers in Alberta who borrowed $9.3 million. In Saskatchewan 72 farmers borrowed $11.4 million. In Manitoba 50 farmers borrowed $6.7 million. In Ontario 237 farmers borrowed $32.5 million. In Quebec 105 farmers borrowed $12.3 million. In the Atlantic region, including all four Provinces, 25 farmers borrowed $2.7 million. The money which has been loaned does not include pending applications.
The breakdown according to enterprise type indicates that on a national basis beef and swine producers have received the biggest share of the funds available. It is that area which is probably the most disorganized of all agriculture in Canada because those producers depend on someone to pay them a fair price for the product that they deliver to the marketplace. Sometimes they wait as long as two weeks to see what they will receive for their product, especially when marketing beef.
We can see what the United States is doing at the present time because of the scare they have over the amount of beef being exported to their country. This meat is being exported mainly by Australia because it had an extra slaughter-kill due to the heavy droughts in that country. That great free marketing system to the south decided to impose a meat import law to stop bringing that slaughter-carcass, broken beef into their country. We were not over our quota but Australia was. The United States decided it would treat all countries in the same fashion, but we were able to negotiate and instead of the quota we would have been given if we were treated similarly to Australia and other countries, with a quota of 101 million pounds, we were allowed to export 120.1 million pounds of beef to the United States. If we had not been able to negotiate that quota we would have been stopped from exporting beef to the United States some time in July or early August, I believe.
So when anyone says that the North American market belongs to us, tell them that they are kidding themselves, because that is what they are doing. The United States is becoming one of the most protected nations in the world. There are approximately 25 bills before Congress presently in the form of protective legislation to attempt to protect their producers of every kind of product imaginable. This is happening in that great, free trading nation to the south, which so many people think it is.
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
A Bill of this nature is not new. In the November 12, 1981 budget the then Minister of Finance announced a similar special program to assist farmers in financial distress. It provided a five percentage point rebate. Similar legislation to this Bill came into force in April, 1982 for the November 12, 1982 special program which terminated on March 31, 1982. There was strong demand for the program, as the statistics indicate. From November 12, 1981, to March 31, 1982, 382 loans totalling $45,417 million were approved. Interest rebates on these loans over a two-year period will total about $4.6 million. The total in the two-year period is approximately $16 million in interest rebates.
I urge Hon. Members to support this Bill which will be instrumental in assisting so many Canadian farmers through these difficult times. Most agriculture producers are at the mercy of the marketplace for their incomes. The price received for their production does not correspond with their costs, and in recent times costs have outstripped earnings for a significant number of our farmers. 1 firmly believe that most of these producers can survive and contribute to the economy if they are given a chance to recover. This interest subsidy for a two-year period provides that breathing room. Agriculture is essential for a healthy economy, and if our economy is to strengthen, so must agriculture.
I want to conclude by pointing out that the number of accounts with the FCC total 75,770 Canadian farmers out of
320,000	farmers. The total number of farmers in default at the present time is approximately 11 per cent. The total amount of loans to all farmers in Canada is close to $4 billion. The amount of money issued under regular loans this year is $252.3 million to date. As I indicated earlier, about $85 million is under the special Farm Financial Assistance Program. We estimate that we will have loaned about $700 million by the time this fiscal year ends. We have made plans and have received applications already, and while we have had several offers, we have not accepted them because we do not think the rates are what we should receive on the American money market. There has been a tender form for approximately $129 million. I am going by memory as to what that figure is.
Average assets of borrowers this year increased by about $368,000. The average loan this year under the regular loans program amounted to $92,400. The average loan issued under the special loans program was $135,000.
Those are just some of the figures that we are using, but we hope that we can use the system to which the Hon. Member referred and which we have discussed, the agribond system. We are still working on it; it has not come through as quickly as I would like to see it. Some of the financial institutions have very strong reservations about it, including the credit unions who say that we would take too much money from their operations. They have expressed strong concern about our proposal for a special system which would allow people to invest with a smaller return on interest by paying no tax on it,

November 4, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
and that type of thing. I still think the principle is good. Other countries are using it. We are still presenting other new proposals to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). I do not know whether the proposal will be ready this year or not, but offers are still regularly coming in, as I said, for long-term money. We do not know what the result of that will be.
As 1 said earlier in my speech, we had refused the proposal of long-term money for a ten-year period, I believe, at 14 per cent interest in Canadian money, which I thought was too high. I am still optimistic that the interest rates will come down and that maybe by Christmas or shortly thereafter the interest rates will be single digit. 1 am very much of an optimist. That will put us in a better position to arrange for longterm money. We are in the best position to arrange long-term money for over two years; but 1 again stress to the House, through Your Honour, that very rarely can one find any institution which will lend long-term money.
As Minister of Agriculture, after listening to what the farm organizations have said to me, I very strongly feel that it is a must that we have long-term financing for farmers. From what we see today on the world commodity markets, the great fluctuations in prices mean that they must have that kind of long-term financing with reasonable rates of interest. This applies to somewhere betwen 35 per cent and 45 per cent of all farmers. Over 50 per cent of our farmers are not in that bracket at all. Farmers in certain age groups do not owe any money, and that takes in nearly 50 per cent of all farmers in Canada. A mixture of grain producers, livestock producers, dairy producers and poultry producers are in that bracket. Some of them have eveii said to me, "Some of your programs, Mr. Whelan, are too rich because we are paying too much income tax at the present time." Well, it is hard in an agricultural community to provide the kind of equity we want. However, if a farmer is paying income tax, that is as it should be, because successful business people pay taxes, and farmers are successful business people. If they are paying taxes, that means they are running very successful, efficient businesses. It is when farmers or business people are not paying taxes that we should worry more about them.
We recently received a visitor to Canada. We showed him the agricultural production entities from Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the different kinds of farm operations that he wanted to see. I know he was very impressed with what he saw. The productive system in our country is so different from the one in his country. He was the minister of agriculture of the Soviet Union, which is our largest purchaser of agricultural products. He wanted to see dry land farming. I was delighted to show him our family type farm operations, from small and medium to the large type operations which have several thousand acres under cultivation. He also saw livestock and grain operations. No other country in the world has a system such as ours.
In reference to the plight of producers in the United States of America, the potato producers of that country requested hearings because they said that they could not compete with the programs available to Canadian producers. Little Canada
was putting the producers out of business in the main potato producing areas of the United States. Hearings were held in Boise, Idaho, and Bangor, Maine. Transcripts of the proceedings are available for anyone to see. However, their main argument was that Canada's programs are so superior to theirs that they cannot compete with us.
Once again I ask for speedy passage of the Bill. I have given a brief report on what we are doing to raise extra funds for the Fram Credit Corporation, but we are being a little bit cautious about arranging long-term money at high rates of interest because we do not want to tie too many farmers into a high rate of interest. I think that no matter who may hold the office of Minister of Agriculture over the next few years, he will have to review mortgages which farmers have taken at 16 per cent or 16.5 per cent interest because the average rate of mortgages is now around 10 per cent on the nearly $4 billion we have out on loan. However, some farmers are paying less than 10 per cent and others are paying 6.5 per cent more than 10 per cent. When they were obtaining those mortgages they were still borrowing money at a rate about five points lower than the regular market rate at that time and they could not obtain long-term mortgages even if they were willing to pay 20 per cent, 21 per cent or 22 per cent interest. That cost us several millions of dollars. However, we think money spent on agriculture is money well spent.
The record of the Farm Credit Corporation and its cost of operation is one of which we are very proud. It is an organization which knows and understands Canadian agriculture, which is one thing the private lending institutions have proven to us they do not understand. By the way, they lent money to the rural community of Canada, but in many cases they did not understand just what was going on. If most of the farmers who are in financial trouble had borrowed long-term money four, five or six years ago from the financial institutions, most of them would not be in such difficulty. We appeal to the private lending institutions to start lending long-term money to the rural community. I can honestly say that I did not realize what they were doing until I became really involved during the last 18 months. Farmers have sent me copies of agreements they have signed with lending institutions. I was amazed, appalled, and in some cases just downright disgusted to find that they had become involved with financial lending institutions which would put them into such difficult positions.
I know that other Hon. Members would like to contribute to the debate, but again I ask for speedy passage of the Bill.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take a great deal of my time to respond to the Minister's opening remarks except to say that I am somewhat surprised that his comments were directed to some of my colleagues and farmer friends in the Province of Alberta. There is certainly no question that farmers who carry on business in Alberta are obviously Canadian farmers, and if there were any doubt in anyone's mind, I simply draw attention to the overwhelming manner in which they voted in the recent provincial election. We find that the Premier was able to gather some 75 out of 79
November 4, 1982

seats and the WCC was completely wiped out of the Legislature.
He also made a reference to the worthiness of the agribond concept. I was certainly encouraged to hear the Minister respond favourably with respect to it because 1 really think it is the only way to go, the only route which would provide sufficient financing at the lowest possible cost to Government. Losses to the Consolidated Revenue Fund would be minimized and it would supply sufficient funds to assist the farmers who find themselves in severe financial difficulties.
There has been some debate as to who should claim credit for the agribond concept. 1 am sure the Minister has tried to lay claim to it, as did my colleague earlier today. As I understand the situation from my reading of history, that concept was born out of a farm meeting held by a group of farmers in the Province of Saskatchewan and was brought to our caucus by the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton). Rather than the Minister or myself taking credit for it, I think we should give credit where it is due. As with most good agricultural programs, this one had its origin at the grass roots level.
I welcome this opportunity to comment on Bill C-134, Mr. Speaker. As Members of the Government will understand, it is not traditional for critics to be overly complimentary but I want to indicate that I am somewhat encouraged by the priority given this Bill by the Government House Leader. Of the three agricultural Bills among the 18 or 19 on the Government's list, the choice of Bill C-134 for debate today is quite proper and a step in the right direction.
While the concept is a good one because it recognizes the problem, the amount of money made available to tackle a problem of this magnitude falls far short of what is needed to do the job properly. The Government knows that when legislation that will assist the agricultural community is introduced, it can expect to receive our co-operation and support. There are many examples of our co-operation on legislation of this type.
Having made those comments honestly and sincerely, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to leave the impression that this rather limited measure will do a great deal to resolve these problems that have plagued the economics of the agricultural industry, particularly during the last 24 months. Throughout this debate, my colleagues and I will demonstrate, by fact and example, that the agricultural industry in Canada is experiencing the worst economic crisis in four decades. Indeed, some knowledgeable people will recognize that the current dilemma in the agricultural industry is probably the worst since Confederation.
Last fall I was invited by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture to serve as a member of a small task force organized to deal with this emergency in agriculture. I accepted the invitation for a number of reasons. I was aware of, and concerned about, the serious financial conditions that were beginning to develop in the industry in the early part of 1981. Last fall, the
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
most seriously affected people were young farmers with sizeable debt loans and those in the red meat industry. Some improvement had taken place in the red meat industry by this fall, but unfortunately it could be short-lived. Certain actions taken by the U.S. Government will exert a downward pressure on beef prices. The increasing number of hogs being produce in Canada means that there will be a greater number on the market within six or eight months, and that will have a depressing effect.
This year, the financial crisis has spread to the cash crop farmers. Three factors have combined to create this impossible situation. First, high interest rates; second, increased input costs; and third, declining market prices. If one examines the history of agriculture it will be seen that one of these factors can usually be found at any time, but when all these factors are combined for an extended period of time, it creates an impossible situation.
It will be recognized that interest rates have declined but, given the traditional and historic profit margins associated with the primary sector of the agricultural industry and our current economic conditions, they remain too high. There has been a dramatic increase in the amount of total Canadian farm debt. In 1960 it was $1.6 billion; ten years later, in 1970, it had increased to $4.2 billion; 9 years later, in 1979, it had increased to $13 billion; in 1981 it was $16 billion; and this year it could go as high as $18 to 20 billion.
Servicing this debt at an interest rate of 8 or 10 per cent, with improved market conditions, could be possible; however, the cost of servicing the debt at today's interest rates is impossible for a large number of Canadian farmers to meet. In 1981, farmers paid out $2.2 billion in interest payments alone. This is almost $600 million more than was paid in 1980. Farm input costs have risen to the extent that net farm income will decline this year by at least 17 per cent and a further decline is projected for 1983.
Statistics Canada estimates that the 25 per cent increase in energy costs will be the major factor in the decline of net farm income. We have to recognize that energy is vital to Canadian food production, Mr. Speaker. In Ontario, about one-third of the total cost of operation of a cash crop farm is taken up by energy. In the greenhouse industry, energy takes about 22 per cent; in the dairy industry it accounts for about 14 per cent, and in the production of beef it accounts for about 7 per cent of the cost.
Some examples of declining market prices include the price of corn. I am sure the Minister is aware that this year corn has been a reasonable crop, selling at about $2.50 per bushel. One has to apply drying charges, of course, which are extremely high. The cost of producing a bushel of corn is not $2.50 nor $3.50, but is closer to $5.50. Large crops of soybeans are produced in Essex County in the Minister's riding, so he should know that soybeans are selling for something in the neighborhood of $6 per bushel when the cost is closer to $8 or $10 per bushel. Other examples could be cited for Ontario grains and for grains grown in western Canada.

November 4, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
The Government has never really given the agriculture industry much priority. We have seen a number of legislative updates but we have not seen any real measures directed to the agrifood industry in the last 10 or 15 years. Regardless of this Government's indifference, the agrifood industry is the most basic and vital industry in this country. It is an industry on which all life and all sectors depend. Canadians, and indeed civilization throughout the world, can do without just about everything except one thing, and that is food.
Some of my urban friends may wonder why we are taking the time we are today to debate agricultural legislation. Some of our urban friends might ask what is their place and their involvement in the agricultural industry. The very simple answer is that if you eat, you are involved in agriculture.
In Canada there are about 300,000 farmers. That number continues to diminish. Those 300,000 farmers provide direct employment for nearly 500,000 people. That is a tremendous number of jobs. There are about 1.5 million Canadians out of work, so it represents a significant contribution toward employment opportunities and job creation which is not being fully utilized. There are approximately 4,000 food and beverage establishments in Canada and they employ over 200,000. That is more jobs. In fact, this sector is the country's largest single employer. Quite often we think of the automobile industry as the largest sector in our economy as far as job creation is concerned. That obviously is not the case.
It is recognized that the agrifood industry constitutes about 40 per cent of Canada's economy and employs about 25 per cent of all Canadians. In 1980 we exported $8 billion worth of food products and imported about $5 billion. This gave Canada a trade surplus of about $3 billion. However, approximately $3.5 billion of the $5 billion worth of imported food could have been replaced by Canadian-grown produce. Consequently, the lack of any real import replacement program has resulted in a loss of economic activity to Canada and a loss of jobs in Canada during a time when we need them most.
The cost squeeze has decreased farm incomes. This in turn has substantially reduced the farmer's buying power. This has forced farmers to reduce their purchases, increase their borrowing, sell off their assets and has caused a bankruptcy rate of 65 per cent, comparing September of this year over September of last year. Many have been forced out of business. Others have simply left their businesses. In fact, in the first nine months of 1982 there were some 316 bankruptcies.
If the present rate continues, this year bankruptcies in the agricultural industry could well reach 500. This sharp decline in net farm income is having a drastic effect on business activities in the downtown areas in every city, town and village across this country. Just talk to the downtown merchants, the boards of trade, chambers of commerce, for verification of this loss of business, Mr. Speaker.
This decline is taking its toll as well in the farm supply sector. Sharp declines are expected in fertilizer and chemical sales and in the supply sector of the industry in 1983. Farm
tractor sales are down some 35 per cent; combine sales are down 56 per cent. Dealers are filing bankruptcies and our major farm machinery manufacturers are fighting for survival. Why? Because net farm income is dropping. Profit margins are diminishing. Interest rates remain too high. Market prices for a number of commodities are below the cost of production. Consequently, farmers are not buying machinery because they simply cannot afford to buy. The ripple effect is lost income, lost business activities and lost economic opportunities for thousands of Canadians.
I said earlier that this Bill goes in the right direction. However, in view of the magnitude of the problem, it will simply not do the job. What we need is, first, a moratorium of short duration on farm bankruptcies, foreclosures and powers of sale. The Minister recognizes this to be a problem; a number of his colleagues do as well. They have spoken in support of this moratorium. However, nothing has been delivered.
We need a greater infusion of capital into the Farm Credit Corporation. I have not said exactly how much money would be required. I know it is more difficult to secure funds from the Consolidated Revenue Fund at a time when you have a $23.6 billion deficit. It is much more difficult than if you had a $10 billion deficit, there is no question about that. The CFA has indicated on a number of occasions that it would require at least $1 billion.
We need an interest rate subsidy greater than what we have provided in Bill C-134, applied on a selective basis for the consolidation of debt. As I look at this Bill, my calculation indicates that there are $216 million in the program, $116 million of which is a reshuffle. If you apply that under the normal lending formula of the 4 per cent interest rate, if the funds are fully lent and the 4 per cent rate is applied, the interest rate subsidy would be about $16 million. We are suggesting a more adequate amount would be in the neighbourhood of $300 million.
How do we reach that figure? It is fairly straightforward. We have approximately $17.6 billion or $18 billion in total farm debt. It is estimated that about one-third of that would be at unmanageable interest rates. When it requires $50 million to lower the interest rate by five percentage points on a billion dollars worht of debt, the final calculation indicates it would require about $300 million to provide adequate funds to reduce that interest rate by five percentages points on that $6 billion.
I talked earlier about the agribond concept. I am encouraged to the extent that the Minister is still talking favourably about it. However, if he takes his direction from the blue chip committee or the Lortie Commission, they brought down a ruling recommending against a policy of this kind. The Minister should remind his colleague the Minister of Finance that the membership of the Lortie Commission does not include one farmer.
We need rationalization and stabilization. As the Minister indicated, the provincial Ministers are meeting at this very moment in Regina. If the Minister could deliver on that
November 4, 1982

promise and deliver those dollars in 1978, I do not know why he cannot do the same thing today. He will have to answer to the provincial Ministers. I am certain they will be here in Ottawa within two or three weeks.
The Minister should look carefully at the recommendations of the task force to which I referred earlier and at the recommendations which were put forth by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. When the report of the meeting of the provincial Ministers meeting in Regina is made, I am sure he will see some similarity between the decision they reach today and the income market insurance program put forward by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture.
Changes are required in the area of capital gains. 1 challenge the Minister simply to match the provisions contained in the Crosbie budget in 1979. We want to restore the incomeaveraging provision and the capital gains reserve. Both of these provisions were removed in the November budget, which was probably the worst budget for industry and the most damaging budget ever to Canadian agriculture.
The other area the Minister should be looking at is an energy tax credit or rebate. Forty per cent of the cost of farm fuels, as the Minister will realize, is in direct federal taxation, and that tax represents about 40 cents a gallon on diesel fuel, and some 60 cents a gallon on gasoline. The CFA have had an opportunity to look at this Bill and their bottom line, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that they have determined the money provided in the Bill is totally and wholly inadequate. They estimate about 10 per cent, or some 20,000 farmers, desperately need the assistance of this rebate. The CFA indicate that only some 500 farmers will actually be assisted under this program.
The CFA have also indicated that we should remind the Minister, particularly the Minister of Finance, that although the small business bond provision has been extended, the banks are using this provision in the same way as they have been using the Farm Improvement Loans Act over a number of years. Although they have the legal authority to lend money under this program and under the small business bond, very few banks are participating to any great extent. It is interesting, as well, Mr. Speaker, to look at some of the comments and further recommendations made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Quoting from some correspondence that i have had from the Federation of Agriculture:
The Government must give authority, and quickly, to the FCC to borrow short-term-three to five years-by the issue of financial instruments, on which interest is tax free, for farmers requiring money at lower interest rates not only for debt consolidation but for essential investment and working capital.
Such lending, though necessarily selective, could be much more generously available than the present subsidized FCC lending, because the interest paid by the producer could not be expensed. This makes it a self-policing policy since borrowing on this basis would not be attractive to farmers whose operations indeed were, or could become, profitable.
This policy can be put into place quickly and effectively under present legislation, as we understand it. It is one that comes with a price tag to Government in forgoing some tax revenues, of course, but it is a small price to pay for
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
sustaining the productivity and the family farm structure of an industry of such fundamental long and short-term importance to the Canadian economy.
I acknowledged earlier that interest rates have fallen. I acknowledged as well that this legislation is going in the right direction. But the fall in interest rates is not sufficient and, for many, that reduction in interest rates comes too late. Those who will benefit by this Bill will be far too few. This Government must decide whether they want a strong, viable agricultural industry or whether they want to continue on the road to disaster, a road of loss of productivity, lost employment opportunities, lost economic activities, becoming more dependent on potentially unreliable, more expensive, poorer quality, food imports.
We believe Canada should be striving for the former, but time is running out. The primary sector of the agrifood industry must receive, and receive now, a more positive, meaningful response from this Government. I am certain that the agricultural industry is not asking for the impossible, because if this Government has money for Dome, Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson, and money to purchase B.P. which obviously is a liability on the treasury of Canada, then we say that it should get its priorities in order and should assist the agricultural industry.
Canadian farmers need action from this Government now and they need it in a form of a temporary, short-term moratorium, increased FCC funding, Agribonds, updating of stabilization. They need capital gains changes, and an energy tax rebate. The results of such measures can and will remove this crisis. These measures will turn this current economic crisis into an opportunity. Canadian farmers have the resources, capacity, desire and the determination to meet this challenge. Action now will ensure the preservation of a strong and prosperous agriculture industry.
I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that when this Government, or any Government, has the agrifood industry back on the road to recovery, then they will also have this nation back on the road to recovery.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on a Bill which will reduce the interest on farm credit loans by 4 per cent for a period of two years. I think this is a necessary short-term move. I am not so certain that it is an adequate response to the need. However, it is an indication of an attempt to address the problem.
The problem is one that I would like to dwell on for just a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, because I think that if we do not go back and look at how we got into this credit difficulty, we cannot properly address the real reasons for bankruptcies, why people are behind in their payments, and why people are selling out because they can no longer survive in agriculture.
I submit that Canadian agriculture, probably since the Second World War but certainly in the last decade and a half, has been under some very severe strains and pressures. These are different strains and pressures from those of the post-war years when the objective was simply to become more efficient and a great many people opted out of agriculture. To some

November 4, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
extent they were pulled out of agriculture because there were jobs in the industrial urban centres that were growing rapidly. But in the last 15 years or so we have seen some moves, partly by Government, both federal and provincial, and partly as a response to those policy moves by Government, which have brought a rapid escalation of agricultural production.
I think that in looking back at our agricultural history we tend to see moves that create a situation where types of farming are made obsolete by deliberate policy moves. To some extent that started off with a clutch of policy changes which included the Farm Credit Corporation being deliberately pulled out of the long-term interest rate and medium-term interest farm loan field.
Farm Credit Corporation had been supplying most of the long-term needs of the farm community, and a good portion of the short-term and intermediate financial requirements of farm communities up until the late 60s. Land prices were relatively stable, production capabilities were pretty well regionalized, people knew where they were on the farm front.
The late sixties and early seventies brought some terrific changes, Mr. Speaker. The federal Government began to ease back on the amount of lending by the Farm Credit Corporation. It proposed to allow the banks into the farm credit field. Along with that there was a drastic change in the federal grain policy. Prior to that most feed grains had been marketed across the country, outside of the Prairies, under the auspices of the Canadian Wheat Board. Therefore, prices were relatively stable and the competitive capability of the different regions was kept more or less equal. But the combination of going to the so-called open market and allowing the large grain merchants and feed mills back into the grain market on an across the country basis, along with allowing the banks into the farm credit field, created a climate which may have looked good to the economists behind the Government front benches because it created the illusion of growth in agriculture, but was in fact a switch in production from some regions of the country to others, financed largely with borrowed money.
As well, provincial Governments got into the act by providing subsidies to encourage those shifts. Sometimes it was straight subsidy, at other times it was subsidized credit. In short, by the end of the 1970s there was a quite visible move of much of the hog production out of the Prairie region into Ontario and the Maritimes to some extent, but largely into Quebec. These two or three policy shifts also encouraged a move to feeding cattle outside of the Prairie region where most of the livestock originates.
There were, Mr. Speaker, some very important economic side effects resulting from these shifts. Luckily there was a sudden surge in demand for grains in that period of time which happened to coincide with the increase in oil prices in about 1973 or 1974. That surge in grain prices and agricultural commodities generally tended to carry the farm community through the last decade. As the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) outlined quite well, they were able to do it while watching farm prices decline, costs increase and farm debt increase at a dramatic pace. That has been outlined today. In 1970 accumulated farm debt was $4.2 billion; in 1979 it was up to $13 billion; in 1981 it was $16 billion.
This has put great pressure on financing in this country. Interest rates rose because other sectors of the economy were doing the same thing, growing at a rapid pace, making large demands on the finances of this country and thereby bidding up interest rates. Consequently, by the end of the decade and into the 1980s, we see that the highest farm expense is interest costs. At the beginning of the 1970s the cost of money was about number eight or number ten in priority, and then suddenly it shot to the fore. Following that is the cost of energy, which had not been a tremendously big farm cost. So farmers were very much in a squeeze situation. Long-term credit at fixed rates was becoming less and less available. The Farm Credit Corporation was supplying a smaller and smaller amount of the requirements for farm credit.
Finally, we got into the 1980s when the new, large and intensified livestock production units were beginning to flounder. There was overbuilding, or alleged overbuilding. The units which has been the traditional sources of supply in other parts of the country had been declared obsolete and had shut down. We had, in effect, an overbuilding of the agricultural industry and we were and are carrying costs which farmers have no way of avoiding.
Banks have been willing and able to supply credit needs up until recently because along with this decade of growth came high inflation in the value of farm land. So every time a banker went to review an individual farmer's account he could usually conclude that, because of the rapid increase in real estate values, the assets still exceeded the liabilities of the individual farmer. But in the last three or four years that picture has changed for a great many operators. Liabilities began to exceed assets.
As the banks foreclosed on some of those operations it created a new situation where the price of farm land is no longer escalating 12 per cent, 15 per cent, or 18 per cent a year. We are now in a situation where there have been foreclosures and bankruptcies and offers to sell on the part of farmers who think they can no longer survive in the industry, and therefore land prices are falling in many corners of the country and are not rising. That is setting the whole industry on a path which could lead to disaster. The banks, because of their past practices, now have to be a little more careful about forcing some operators into bankruptcy. They are now beginning to realize-if they do not, they should-that the more bankruptcies they cause, the lower will go the price of real estate. The more loans they will have to call because more and more accounts will find themselves in the position of having greater liabilities than assets, since the banks are putting pressure on the real estate market and pushing down the value of those assets.
So what we have before us here is a very feeble attempt to deal with this very grave problem, a problem which I do not
November 4, 1982

think the Minister fully realizes he is faced with. In fact, he even seems to be prepared to create another kind of massive adjustment of agriculture resources by his apparent support for abolishing the Crow rate, which will, in effect, reverse some of the changes we went through in the last decade. This will increase the already high bankruptcy rate in Quebec, the Maritimes and Ontario, just so that a few highly intensive feeding operations in western Canada may get an advantage. I do not think the industry will appreciate that kind of disruption yet again, and that is one of the reasons we have been asking that everybody involved in the process take a second look at it. It will have violent repercussions across the country and in all agricultural sectors of Canada.
The proposal before us is one which has been described as being able to handle a few hundred farmers who are on the line between bankruptcy and survival and to whom a 4 per cent reduction in interest rates for two years might make the difference between survival and collapse.
I think this is important because the bankruptcy rate has been growing by leaps and bounds. In 1979 there were 82 farm bankruptcies in Canada. In 1980 they had doubled to 164. They rose again in 1981 to 191, and so far in 1982-and we are only three-quarters of the way through the year-there have been 316 bankruptcies.
The outlook is not particularly good this year. At the beginning of the year Agriculture Canada predicted that net farm incomes would be down again, the second or third year in a row. Indeed, when we go back as far as 1974 we find that net farm incomes have varied only a little from about $3.5 billion. This year they will be below that figure. If we relate that to 1974 dollars, we can conclude that net farm incomes are less than half at the present time. This is the real reason there is a farm credit crunch. It stems from a disruption of the industry. Large investments have been made in some parts of the country and investments in other parts of the country had to be abandoned. Also it stems from an increase in the demand for funds which has caused interest rates to go sky high and has left farmers with virtually no options.
The Farm Credit Corporation has attempted to increase its finances by going to foreign markets. To date my information is that no funds have been raised in that manner. This coming winter we will probably see great demands for long-term, fixed interest rate loans through agencies such as the FCC. Basically it is the only agency available to farmers which offers longterm, fixed interest rate loans. Interest rates are now going down, but FCC rates are locked into a formula used by FCC which comes down very slowly. The formula was just revised at 15.75 per cent, but farmers can walk into their local credit union or bank and obtain money at lower interest rates because they are still reaping the benefits, if we can call them benefits, of the high interest rates which have gone before.
If the FCC succeeds in obtaining funds from foreign sources at much lower rates than 15.75 per cent, those sums could not be re-lent to farmers at less than that rate until the new
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
formula comes out next spring. Farmers are locked into the situation. The response has been multitudinous. Some Provinces have responded by getting into the farm loan field in which most of them have been involved in some form or another. The demand has increased the intervention of provincial Governments through the offering of sometimes greatly subsidized farm loans to farmers.
If we are to have any stability in the Canadian agricultural community, it is imperative for the Farm Credit Corporation to be enlarged again to provide the long-term, fixed rate credit required by farmers in a volume which will service all requirements across the country. Failure to do so continues the instability in agriculture, instability created when one Province lends money at 5 per cent, another Province lends money at 8 per cent and the going rate on the market is 15 per cent. This creates a tendency for production to shift from regions of comparative advantage to other regions.
I would be remiss if I did not point out that there is a great need for money to finance intergenerational transfers. This is where a good chunk of farm credit funding goes at the present time. Some of it still goes to improving physical plant, but most of it is for transferring land and property from one generation to the next. This amount has been shrinking through FCC and, consequently, other methods have been proposed. The agribond proposal has been around for approximately five or six years. It was discussed in the House and in the Standing Committee on Agriculture several times since I have been here.
Some experiments with turning over land from one generation to another have been tried in various Provinces. There are land banks and land assembly systems in some Provinces which make it possible for the older generation to turn over land under very reasonable terms to the younger generation without their being placed under a debt load which they cannot handle and enabling them to produce under current market conditions.
Such programs should be reviewed and looked at objectively, but I think we should come to the conclusion that the FCC must be expanded if Canadian agriculture is to have an equal chance right across the country. If we are to have an agrifood policy which takes advantage of what is on the farms now and makes it possible for production units to produce in a market that provides some stability, farmers will increase production and help the country out of the current economic chaos. If stabilization programs are available on a federal basis, and if marketing systems are in place which provide some equity across the nation, then farmers will have some assurance that by producing they will be able to get back their costs of production plus decent standards of living for their families.
The proposal before us today is a very short-term one to help a few hundred farmers. I have no objection to that, but I should like to point out that there are thousands and thousands more who will need equal consideration. This proposal, while of assistance to a few hundred, is only a drop in the bucket in terms of meeting the total need.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) mentioned earlier, the federal Farm Financial Assistance Program was established in order to alleviate the distressing situation created by high interest rates and lower returns on farm products. Canadian farmers who are facing serious financial difficulties can obtain an interest rebate of four percentage points on their loans for two years, which reduces the effective interest cost to 11 % per cent during the first two years of the loan. The Program has already saved several hundred farmers from bankruptcy, and will probably save several hundred more before it expires.
The Farm Credit Corporation has always done its utmost to help its clients through difficult periods. Its recovery plans, for instance, are among the most flexible known. FCC credit advisers encourage farmers to discuss their financial difficulties as soon as they become apparent, so that they can then reconsider repayment schedules and take appropriate action. In some cases, rescheduling of the loan may be necessary. In others, postponement of one or two payments may be sufficient. It is reassuring to note, however, that the FCC is sufficiently concerned about the problems facing its clients to take this kind of action, and that this agency, which represents the Government, has not forgotten the human factor in its business relations with Canadian farmers. In addition to its flexible recovery plans and the special loans being granted since June 1982 under the Special Farm Financial Assistance Program, the FCC offers its borrowers every opportunity to resolve their financial problems through its Advisory Services Program.
Generally speaking, all FCC loan applicants may benefit from preliminary counselling, including advice on how to organize and develop their farm operations. The service is available to any FCC borrower who asks for it. However, the service is compulsory in the case of borrowers under the special program, since it is one of the conditions of the loan. If we look at the components of this Program, it is easy to understand why the service is compulsory for borrowers who are in financial difficulty and are anxious to improve their situation. First of all, the goal of the Advisory Services Program is to help the farmer manage his farm finances more effectively. The credit adviser will therefore help the farmer to select the accounting system that is best adapted to his needs and help him get acquainted with the system. With his financial training and experience, the credit adviser is also in a position to help the farmer interpret and analyze the financial data provided by his accounting system. He can also provide a comparative analysis of financial factors and farm production in similar operations. Finally, if the farmer requires another adviser, the credit adviser can tell him where to obtain the information or the help he needs. Thus, this service is an adjunct to provincial educational programs.
As a result of the follow-up provided through the Advisory Services Program, the farmer has a better chance of successfully implementing his recovery plan. Thus, Mr. Speaker, the FCC is doing everything in its power to help borrowers through the difficult times we are experiencing today. By supporting Bill C-134, my hon. colleagues will enable the FCC to continue its good work. Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize that Canadian agriculture is represented by a very large percentage of family farms, and I would like to quote a few figures here to underline the importance and growth of Canadian agriculture. According to the 1981 census, there were 366,000 farms in 1971 and there were only 318,000 in 1981. However, although the number of farms has dropped significantly, there has been, conversely, an increase in production.
Last week, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) made his speech in the House, he mentioned the high productivity of our farmers and was happy to see that this group had continued to progress and to provide the Canadian consumer with products at very reasonable cost. I cannot agree more with the words of the Minister of Finance, and here I would like to underline the importance of Canadian agriculture and its productivity.
I want to give a few statistics on the assets of our agricultural sector and thus illustrate the need for the measures being proposed in Bill C-134. I am sure that honourable members will realize that many farmers need financial assistance and some are facing more difficult conditions at a time when the economy is deteriorating in certain sectors, and also that it is absolutely necessary to help farmers cope with these temporary problems. Thus, in 1971, the average farm was worth $65,800; in 1981, average farm assets had risen to $409,300. On the basis of these figures, you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer's financial requirements are increasing steadily. Of course, the debt rate has also followed this trend. In 1971, the average farm debt was $12,600, and in 1981, it was $58,000. My point is, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer needs more support, because while in 1971, our agriculture was worth $4,500 billion, by 1981, this figure had increased to $18 billion, which represents an annual increase of 15.1 per cent. Also, farmers are playing a very important role in our economy, since we are exporting increasing amounts of farm products to world markets, which is an invaluable asset to our trade balance. Mr. Speaker, I do not think Bill C-134 needs further justification, and once again 1 hope that the bill will pass all stages in the House and that we will then be able to help farmers in financial difficulty by providing an interest rebate.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am among those today who speak with reservation in favour of Bill C-134. This Bill does not receive my wholehearted endorsement. Like so many measures emanating from this
November 4, 1982

beleaguered Government, it is a half measure. It is part of a half-baked and ill-conceived range of policies, in this particular instance dealing with agriculture financing, a subject that has been an issue in this country for as long as I can remember.
For many years I was a practising veterinarian in the beef cattle country of central British Columbia. In this, and in other capacities 1 have been in continual contact with cattle producers and have become very familiar with their problems.
A subject that is continually raised is financing; how to finance the purchase of property, livestock and equipment. Of course, the pros and cons of the Farm Credit Corporation are often discussed. The most common complaint that we hear in my part of the world is that a person is lucky if he can get a Farm Credit Corporation loan because usually the Corporation is out of money. In B.C., farmers and ranchers have pretty well given up looking to Ottawa for financial assistance. I do not expect that attitude to be changed very much as a result of this Bill, legislation that will affect perhaps only 500 farmers in Canada and maybe 25 or 30 in British Columbia. The agricultural community in my province looks mainly to the provincial Government for help when needed.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext: We pay twice as much in B.C. to agriculture as they do. Where are they getting their help? They are getting it from us.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
The Province of British Columbia has had an interest rebate plan in place for many years and has assisted a good many producers of agricultural commodities. Last year there were 5,700 applicants for this Program. The B.C. Government also provides guarantees for agricultural loans. If you ask any farmer or rancher what is needed most in Canadian agriculture today, I will wager that nine out of ten will say: "Just give us some long-term money at a reasonable, fixed rate of interest and then leave us alone." Of course, today this cry issues forth from all sectors of the economy, but I venture to say that farmers have been saying it for the longest time.
Further, the question of finance and credit is a vital issue to young people trying to take their rightful place in Canadian agriculture. The average age of Canadian farmers today is 49, and obviously young people must be encouraged to take the place of those who retire. It is almost impossible these days for them to do this unless they are fortunate enough to inherit a farm or ranch. Even if this does happen, there is no guarantee that the operation will remain viable.
There is no doubt that there is a real need for reasonable credit, and there is no doubt that the Farm Credit Corporation requires a larger pool of capital. Presently there is a plan afoot to raise $100 million in the United States by selling notes on U.S. exchanges. We are assured that U.S. insurance companies, both fire and general, and pension fund agents will eagerly line up to purchase Canadian securities in the form of Farm Credit Corporation notes. It is my understanding that this offering will be forthcoming when brokers feel that
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
conditions are stable and top prices can be obtained for the issue. Perhaps now that the United States mid-term elections are behind us, we will soon see these notes on U.S. markets. Naturally, foreign exchange and interest rates are vital considerations in this scheme. At present, Canada's dollar, at 82.5 cents U.S., will add a full 2 per cent to the 12 per cent cost of this money, 12 per cent being the approximate U.S. interest rate.
In order to protect itself from foreign exchange risk, the U.S. money raised and returned to Canada will have to be hedged. This will likely add a further cost of about 2 per cent, and allowing 1 per cent for Farm Credit Corporation administration, the money would finally reach the borrower at a cost of 17 per cent-not what I or anyone else would call cheap money. Is this, then, the purpose of Bill C-134, to reduce the interest rate and thus the flak that the Corporation and the Government would have to bear for procuring expensive foreign money?
As I understand it, the plan is to lend this money to Canadian farmers at a fixed rate of interest over a ten-year period. An obvious risk to the Farm Credit Corporation could occur in the event that loans are prepaid before full term, when the Corporation could be left with some pretty expensive money on its hands. Farmers have expressed concern over the Farm Credit Corporation venturing into foreign currency markets, worried that the plan might fail and make loans even more expensive. Many have rightfully asked, "Why not raise the needed funds at home in Canada?"
It seems to me that Canadians would be most interested in supporting Canadian agriculture through purchasing Canadian agricultural bonds. Our Party has long advocated the establishment of an agribond, as was mentioned earlier this afternoon by my colleague the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise).
For years and years this Government has neglected to address the serious problem of adequately financing Canadian agriculture. The Farm Credit Corporation over these years has been literally stangled by lack of sufficient capital to lend. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Government know full well how the lack of capital at a reasonable rate, especially for long-term credit, has throttled Canadian agriculture. Why has the Minister not made this problem his top priority instead of such things as threatening beef producers with his ridiculous and destructive plan for a beef marketing board? Why is he spending so much energy flogging the abomination called Canagrex? He and his colleagues might saddle Canada with Canagrex, but if they cannot properly finance our farmers, young and old, then it will not be very long until there is little, if anything, to export to other countries.
Over the years I have had many opportunities to discuss agricultural financing with American ranchers who have moved to Canada. I cannot remember one who was not completely dismayed by the evident lack of credit options

November 4, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
available to Canadian farmers. Many told me of a very popular institution in the United States called Production Credit Associations. They could not understand why Canada did not provide a similar option. 1 am indebted to the Canadian Cattlemen's Association for providing me with information on Production Credit Associations.
The PCAs originated under the Federal Farm Loan Act of 1916 in the United States. In 1933, PCAs became retail outlets for credit available at wholesale from the federal intermediate credit banks. At first, their equity base was supplied by Government funding. Later, as the Government money was paid off, the equity base was supplied by Association members. Equity is in the form of class A and class B shares. All borrowers must be shareholders. When obtaining a loan the borrower has to invest 5 per cent to 10 per cent in class B stocks. No interest or dividends are paid on this class B stock. Once the loan is repaid, the borrower can allow his equity to remain in the PCA to provide a fund base for future loans. If the member does not borrow for two years his class B shares are converted to class A and a dividend is paid.
PCAs use their equity base to borrow from the federal intermediate credit banks of which there are 12 in the United States. They raise their funds through the sale of securities to investors in the nation's money markets. PCAs pay state and federal taxes. Their structure is basically that of a farmer-owned co-operative with a board of directors made up of active member borrowers. The administrative cost of loans is one-half of 1 per cent and interest on loans is usually 2 per cent to 4 per cent below commercial bank prime rates in the United States.
I have a brochure provided to me by the Production Credit Association and I would like to quote some of the significant points mentioned:
Are PCAs Providing Government Loans to Farmers?
No, all government funds originally in PCAs were completely paid back. The PCAs are now all farmer owned.
Who Operates Local Associations?
Only farmers who borrow money from PCA are permitted to become members and owners. Only these members have the power to elect members to serve on the board of directors.
What Prompted the Organization of PCA?
Necessity! Prior to its founding, farmers often found themselves without an adequate source of credit that was dependable. Also, the terms and conditions of the credit did not work to the best advantage of the farmer. PCA, by providing a reliable, permanent source of funds, has eliminated most of these credit problems for farmers and ranchers.
What Additional Advantages Does PCA Offer?
It is operated for farmers by farmers-who understand the needs and problems involved in farming as well as farm credit. In addition, through the Federal Intermediate Credit Banks, PCA has ready access to funds from the nation's money markets.
More Specifically, For What Purposes Can Loans Be Made?
For feed, seed, fertilizer, labor, harvesting expenses, fencing and other improvements, chemical sprays, spraying equipment, farm and home supplies; money to buy livestock, poultry, machinery processing equipment, storage facilities-
In short, practically anything the farmer needs to produce food.
How Much Can Be Borrowed From PCA?
Practically any amount. Loans are based on the amount needed to do the job; how much can be used profitably; the amount of dependable income from the operation for which the loan is made.
How Much Time Does it Take to Get a Loan?
The time varies from a few minutes for established members to perhaps up to 1 week for a new member.
Who Passes on Loan Applications?
The member-elected board of directors names two of its members to serve with the association's manager on a loan committee. These two members and the manager review the applications.
Besides PCAs there are several other options available in the U.S., such as the federal land banks, local banks and the Bankers Acceptance Corporation, just to mention three. Original sources of credit similar to what I have just outlined are desperately required by Canadian agriculture. If Canadian farmers were ever presented with a brochure similar to the one I have just been quoting from, I am certain their first reaction would be one of the total disbelief. Fighting to get financed in Canadian agriculture has become a way of life.
Canada is light years behind in the financing of its agricultural sector. The Farm Credit Corporation does the best it can under the terms imposed upon it by Liberal politicians who continue to fail to come to grips with this very serious problem.
