speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after a few weeks in our constituencies where we were able to determine the needs of our constituents, listen to them and discuss the economic future of our regions and our own ridings, I am glad to be back in the House with my colleagues to deal with the issues raised by various Members. First of all, we now have before us a motion introduced by a Member, and I believe it is one of the most important aspects of our democracy that, regardless of their political party, private Members can express their opinions by introducing bills and defend the views of their constituents, as the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) is now doing.
November 4, 1982

For my part, I have already spoken on the matter under consideration for about ten minutes. During our first discussion, I explained that it is extremely important, when a government, such as the Government of Canada, negotiates with a company, whether Cargill or any other, that these negotiations remain confidential. Because of the competition between the various companies in all economic sectors throughout the country, such companies cannot afford to make public their financial statements or economic situation simply because they are negotiating with the Canadian Government to obtain certain grants. It would not be normal for such information to be made public and for the competitors of these companies to learn about their financial situation. The important thing for the Canadian taxpayer is that his tax dollars be redistributed equitably among the various regions, that everything be done legally and that after the money is redistributed and the grant is promised, the people be informed of the reasons for the grant, namely to create so many jobs or to promote the economic development of such a sector or such an area. This is a far cry from divulging all the figures requested by the Hon. Member. To quote from motion No. 87, he asks that telephone costs, communications and the correspondence between the company and DREE be made public. In all my three years as assistant to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and my two years as executive assistant, Mr. Speaker, 1 have never known such information to be made public because, as I was saying, it is extremely important for the companies involved that if they have developed, for instance, specific working procedures or development plans for their company, these not be made public only because they had to provide them to the Government to establish the profitability of their business. That is why I have to remind the Hon. Member for Mackenzie that, while I find it extremely laudable on his part to defend the views of his constituents and to work for the welfare of his riding, the company involved in this matter took certain steps because it wanted to improve its facilities, but in the belief that the Canadian Government would keep in mind that its assets, its development program and its financial statement are its own business and that of its shareholders and not something that should be made available to the public tomorrow morning. I want to make myself clear, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I am repeating myself. If the Canadian Government gives even one penny to someone, it is normal that the Canadian people know where this penny went and why. That I admit. But I stronghy object to all information submitted by Canadian citizens or Canadian companies being made public simply because the latter are dealing with the government. I think that is going a bit too far. Besides, the purpose of the whole exercise is definitely not to open the books of those companies for public viewing, but rather to help them prosper so that people in general will be better off in the end. Such is the purpose of regional development legislation and, I would suggest, of current negotiations between the company and the Department. Some people may say that the Department
Dree Grant
expects too much but I for one am glad that it does so. Being aware of the very high number of grants awarded by the Department, and of the substantial amounts involved in certain cases, I would rather not see all those funds redistributed haphazardly to the various areas of the country. It is quite normal for the Department to insist on profitability and, in that respect, the rate of failure among companies which were given assistance by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is very low, even lower than the rate where banks are involved. This is important because that happens to be the taxpayers money. It pays the Government to help a company with public funds, provided that company is operational and creates jobs which will generate income for the state as well as for the people living close to the company plant.
Mr. Speaker, our regional economic development legislation has been extremely useful over the past 15 years because it has played a major role, particularly in a riding such as mine, in the development of various industries, whether small, medium or large. The presence of the Department has been quite evident, particularly in areas where economic development was lagging. In these trying times, a number of companies which had been given assistance by DREE are now the only economic mainstay of certain regions now experiencing very serious difficulties.
That is why I urge the Hon. Member for Mackenzie to keep in mind the spirit and the principle of that legislation which was designed to help certain companies in certain regions, not everywhere, because those regions do need an economic stimulus. Even so, those companies must indeed be assured that their operations and their economic standing will not be the object of public scrutiny.
Those are the remarks I wanted to make on this subject, Mr. Speaker. I hope they will enlighten my colleagues, at least so they will know what DREE is all about and why discretion is the order of the day. Personally, I hope the Department will keep up the good work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend a few moments discussing this motion to make public papers regarding a DREE grant, or lack of a DREE grant, to the Cargill Grain Company to build an oil seed crushing plant at Melfort, Saskatchewan.
What seems to be have been involved was an application by the Cargill Company for a $2 million DREE grant for a plant to be built costing in the neighbourhood of $25 million. Apparently the grant was not forthcoming and therefore the plant was not built.
I would like to spend some time discussing the circumstances behind the rapeseed industry. First, I want to comment on the freedom of information argument made by the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) in the debate last May. He suggested this was a clear-cut case for a freedom of

information Bill and that such a Bill would be useful in the circumstance. There are some laudable uses for a freedom of information Bill.
1 am certain that regardless of what Government implemented a Freedom of Information Act or provided the House with such a Bill, a certain amount of information would still not be made public for a number of reasons. I can see that agencies of Governments engaging in business in competition with other corporations around the world would be very loth to produce all information of how they arrived at a certain price, or how they achieved a certain business agreement. 1 think specifically of the Canadian Wheat Board. A great many Prairie farmers would be hurt badly if the Canadian Wheat Board was forced to provide all relevant information regarding business dealings because their competitors are not forced, in any jurisdiction around the world, to make that same kind of information public.
1 doubt any Government or Party would be absolutely free and forthcoming with information. For example, I simply point to the Official Opposition, whose Party has been loudly in the forefront asking for freedom of information legislation and has been a champion of this legislation for some years. This is the same Party that refuses to make its platform public. They say this will happen when the time for an election comes. Until then it is top secret information. I can understand that, and so can a lot of businesses and Government agencies, but the Progressive Conservative Party has imposed definite limits to its freedom of information when it comes to its political plans, even though it is the kind of information that most voters in Canada would be interested in since it is part of the full and efficient functioning of any democracy.
On the question of rapeseed crushing plants in the Melfort area, the question of building more crushing capacity several years ago seemed to be a fairly good business decision. In retrospect, we can see and understand why Cargill did not proceed, since they were going to be putting up over 90 per cent of the capital, in any case. We can understand why they did not when we see what the industry is faced with. I know that Cargill has one of the best market divisions in the world. It is probably the largest grain handling and grain marketing and processing institution in the world at this time. In the intervening two or three years, we have seen that we do not need more crushing capacity, given current market conditions. There is a surplus of crushing capacity in western Canada now, given the price of oil. There are, I suppose, two and a half plants in Saskatchewan, at Nipawin, at Saskatoon and one at Lloydminster balanced on the Alberta-Saskatchewan border.
We are now in a position in that part of the country where most of the crushers are crying that they have not been generating great profits. There were some profitable years, but those have gone. In fact, crushers in Manitoba and Saskatchewan are now crying foul because of a move by the Province of Alberta which has offered the industry $40 per tonne of rapeseed crushed, up to 90 per cent of last year's crushing volume, in order to keep the industry in Alberta growing and
in an effort to concentrate more of the industry in that Province. As well there are subsidies in Alberta, tank car leases, which have increased from the old subsidy rate of 70 per cent of cost to what will now become 90 per cent of cost in the coming year.
So we begin to see some of the problems that have developed in the rapeseed crushing industry since this application first began. The production of rapeseed has not been increasing and there are a number of reasons for that; one is world conditions. The world oil seed output has been reduced, but prices are still under much pressure, again, in part, because of interference by various government. The European Economic Community is offering what to Canadian farmers seems like massive subsidies in order to export rapeseed to countries like Japan, which is our main buyer of raw seed.
Internally, our marketing system has been undergoing some turmoil. As many members in the House will know, rapeseed is marketed through the open market with the Winnipeg Grain Exchange selling and buying futures. A great many small and medium-sized operators in the market are handling the rapeseed and providing a brokerage function between the farmer and the final user.
There has been some change to the Cinderella crop in the last three or four years in the domestic market as well. It is not just the problem of selling the oil and doing the crushing, but there have been internal marketing problems as well. The market was being dominated by a growing number of small grain buyers, and producer confidence in those buyers has been severely shaken over the last three or four years by a number of dramatic and very well publicized bankruptcies, which have left farmers holding the bag for the costs. Farmers have lost on each of these bankruptcies anywhere from a few million to quite a few million dollars because of the method used in handling farmer rapeseed.
These companies are fairly numerous. Anyone who reads the grain news in western Canada knows about the Memco bankruptcy, the Econ Consulting bankruptcy and Diversified. Others that created a problem were Consolidated Seed Exports, and Gibb Farms Limited at Elm Creek also took down quite a few farm dollars with it when it went down, and Trans-Canada Marketing Service in Manitoba took with it a lot of farmers' money as well. There is some hesitancy, therefore, by farmers to produce rapeseed because of the uncertainty in the market and the kinds of operators that have been coming forward.
The disintegration and multiplicity of the market has created some problems for the buyers also. There are only a few large companies buying out of Japan. When they try to purchase it is sometimes difficult to assemble a full shipload. In order to do that, there are often fairly high premiums paid on carload lots of rapeseed waiting on track in Vancouver. Sometimes it is impossible for any one broker to provide buyers with the quantity of products which they need. For this reason there has been some continuing agitation on the part of farmers to have the whole question of marketing of rapeseed

*
November 4, 1982

handled through the Canadian Wheat Board so that there is one agency amassing the grain and forwarding it, in order to deal adequately with the few large buyers of rapeseed and the Japanese Food Commission which, as I said before, is our biggest customer.
So the Cinderella crop has got to the point where, even though we had developed the crop with very sophisticated research, we were world leaders in genetic selection of rape-seed, world leaders in providing, manufacturing and developing the kind of equipment which would test the genetic potential of the varieties produced; and even though we were also at the leading edge of developing varieties which would provide very specific oil qualities required by the trade with very specific types of protein and amino-acids in the meal which went with the rapeseed, we have been having some difficulty finding markets. I think this is in part because, while the industry has done a good job of concentrating its research and production abilities, it has neglected the marketing end which I think is probably the area which needs full attention at this point in time.
I realize that in backing the introduction of one more crushing plant in western Canada, the Hon. Member for Mackenzie realizes what an advantage a crushing plant would be to the largest centre in his riding and is aware of the economic advantages which would spin off from that. But I think we must also recognize the over-all problems the industry is facing which have caused a major company like Cargill to avoid building a plant, given those economic conditions.
We have no objection to the papers being made public if there is anything to be made public. I think though, in retrospect, several years having passed since this application was begun, most of us can see the economic situation-that probably the marketing people in Cargill had foreseen, which was probably far more important to that company than the availability or not of less than 10 per cent of the total cost by way of a DREE grant. We would be prepared to see the papers produced, but I think we understand the economics behind the program not going forward.

Now, in the present case, the minister responsible for DREE at the time, the Hon. Member for Matane (Mr. De Bane), wrote to the Hon. Member, giving him a very specific answer regarding the refusal of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Regional Economic Expansion, which was DREE at the time, and this letter, which is dated November 2, 1981, is very clear. It says very explicitly, and I quote:
After an exhaustive review of the case, I feel confident that Cargill can, and will, proceed with the project without assistance from DREE. The company is financially strong and the project appears to be a wise one from the company's point of view.
That was written in this letter, which also said that in view of the fact that Cargill Grain Limited could afford to carry out its project without Government funds there seemed to be no reason to grant money to a corporation which can manage on its own. Besides Cargill Grain Ltd applied under the special regional development legislation which quite clearly states that the department may grant funds only to such corporations which really need financial assistance. So far,-and here opinions may differ-experts in this area have felt that Cargill Grain Limited can afford to build its own plant without help. On receiving an application, Department officials investigate thoroughly to make sure the need is genuine. In this case, the Hon. Member is aware that Departmental officials had several meetings with Cargill's representatives to find out what could be done under the current development legislation. The hon. member is also aware that the Minister must abide by the law just as any other Parlimentarian or citizen. Even if the Minister had wanted to grant the funds requested by Cargill he could not have on the basis of the financial statements, which show a satisfactory balance sheet and also on account of the fact that the available funds can only be used on a short-term basis. If the Minister had done otherwise, he would have acted illegally.
The documents and the reply enclosed in the letter which was given to the hon. members are quite clear. 1 suggest that this motion is much more dilatory than real. Perhaps the Hon.

November 4, 1982
Dree Grant
Member should use a different procedure to bring it up or choose another course of action for instance, he could get from Cargill the documents he is seeking from the Department, because the Department is not authorized to reveal the financial interests of private corporations. And I think that any Member of this Elouse would recognize the legitimacy of this principle. Cargill has never agreed to allow the Government to release its financial statements or the nature of its application or its financial requirements. Such a request has never been made by Cargill, and if the Hon. Member ever wanted to know more about this matter, the best way for him would be to prevail upon Cargill to make this information available to him.
When the Hon. The Minister once again replied to the Hon. Member specifying that the Cargill case in Quebec City was entirely different from the Cargill project in Melfort, Saskatchewan. He has a chance then to discuss these matters with the authorities of the Department. I think that the Minister's explanations with respect to the Regional Development Incentives Act were quite clear. This is what the Hon. Member should keep in mind and he should not think that the Department is denying grants at whim on the grounds that they would be unreasonable. However, the Department cannot provide a grant because the application does not meet the criteria set forth in the legislation. And this is the fact on which is based the Department's decision. We would be the first to be blamed if the Department were to start distributing funds to companies or corporations which definitely do not need them. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to enter into the debate. Unfortunately I only have five minutes. I would have very much liked to inform Hon. Members of a number of items which the Government of Canada has done for the oil seed crushing industry, but because of the time limitation I will
stick to the specific motion of the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski).
I am somewhat surprised that the Hon. Member would request an order which would violate the basic business and trade ethics of providing information on a transaction with a company when public funds have not been granted. I want to make my position clear that it is not possible or proper to agree to the request of the Hon. Member for making confidential documents public. 1 am unaware of a time where information of a confidential commercial nature was disclosed to Parliament prior to the file either being processed or a positive decision being reached. I will elaborate on this further. However, I want to respond first to what I believe is the concern which precipitated the request of the Hon. Member, that of the Department's processing of the Cargill application for an RDIA grant.
The matter of the Cargill application has received considerable attention and analysis by officials within my Department. I am well aware of the extensive media coverage and the representations which have been made to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) and to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), former ministers of DREE, and their officials on behalf of the proposed Cargill project at Melfort.
With respect to the proposed project, I appreciate the importance of enhancing value-added processing in Saskatchewan and recognize that support of the agricultural processing industry in Saskatchewan would have a significant impact upon the provincial economy. It is appreciated that if the Cargill oil seed crushing plant were to proceed, there would be the potential for benefits in the long-term benefits to Canada, benefits to the Province of Saskatchewan, to agricultural producers and to the City of Melfort.
The Government's support and recognition of a strong, stable oil seed crushing industry in Canada is evidenced by the favourable ruling of the Federal Investment Review Agency which approved Cargill's proposal to establish an oil seed crushing facility in Melfort, Saskatchewan.
As was indicated to the Hon. Member on May 27, 1982, by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Maltais), the original decision not to provide a DREE grant to Cargill was based on the judgment that Cargill was financially strong and the belief that the project would proceed without assistance from DREE. I believe it is worthwhile at this time to review the facts as outlined to the House on May 27. The Parliamentary Secretary quoted from a letter sent to the Hon. Member from the then minister of DREE, the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Again because I feel it is important, I should like to quote from that letter dated November 2, 1982. In part it read:
After an exhaustive review of the case, I feel confident that Cargill can, and will, proceed with the project without assistance from DREE. The company is financially strong and the project appears to be a wise one from the company's point of view.
November 4, 1982

The letter went on to indicate that since Cargill Grain Limited had the financial resources to carry out its project without Government funding, it would perhaps be inappropriate on the part of the Government to provide funds to a company which already had the means to carry out its project independently.
The legislation regarding the Regional Development Incentives Act is clear. It authorizes the Department to grant funds to a company, provided it can demonstrate a real need. At the time the analysis of the application took place, the firm conclusion was that Cargill Grain Limited was capable of building its plant without a DREE grant and would do so. Thus the Minister, on the evidence submitted, was not authorized to grant funds to Cargill.
At stated in the House previously and repeatedly, the Department is prepared to consider another application from Cargill for the Melfort project at any time. A favourable response to any such application would of course require, in part, that Cargill present a convincing and reasonably attractive projection for the late 1980s and the 1990s for canola crushers as well as demonstrate its need for public assistance on the project. Let me repeat that those specific conditions as well as others are required under the RDIA legislation now, as in the past.
I have attempted in my comments here to provide information which is informative and at the same time respectful of the confidential nature of the transactions that have occurred between Cargill and the Government of Canada.
The provision of copies of correspondence, communications and other documents relating to Cargill's application for RDIA assistance would be contrary to acceptable procedures in Canada and in the international community because of the need to ensure commercial confidentiality. Publishing of this information would be seriously damaging to any future communication between the public and private sectors and is, accordingly, to be resisted. The Department is not allowed to make public statements on private financial interests, and I am sure Members of the House will agree that this is a sound and essential principle.
1 wish to reiterate that to divulge such information could be detrimental to the company, to future RDIA applicants, and to all business and Government transactions based upon the trust in confidentiality. Therefore, I ask that my hon. colleague reconsider and withdraw his motion for these papers.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the consideration of the Chief Government Whip. We are namesakes and we enjoy some camaraderie across the floor. I enjoy having him in the Chamber this evening. I hope he will enjoy what I am going to say about some of the things his Government has been doing. As 1 started to say before five o'clock, this is a very important piece of legislation we are dealing with, first of all because it deals with what I believe to be the most basic industry that Canada has, agriculture, and, second, because it deals with a part of the industry which I believe is fundamental to the agricultural industry maintaining its productivity, and that is the financial end of agriculture. Many years ago, you did not need to have all the financing and sophisticated tools which Canadian agriculture needs today to be productive, but what has happened over the years is that Canadian agriculture has become very capital-intensive. Now, according to figures I have seen recently, it takes more dollars invested in agriculture to create a job than invested in the manufacturing industry in this country. That, by way of explanation, is why the financial problems which Canadian agriculture faces, are so basic to the fundamental problems of the whole Canadian economy. Without a productive agriculture, we are going to find it very difficult to maintain the standard of living we are accustomed to. When we get to a situation where the consumer at large has to spend a larger percentage of his disposable dollars on food, there are less consumer dollars to be spent on other items. That is not a healthy situation to be in. It means that other manufacturing areas of the economy will suffer because there simply would not be as many dollars to be spent on commodities other than food.
The financial end of agriculture, then, becomes very important to the total economic picture, not only for domestic reasons, but also because of what agriculture does on the export market. Agriculture is a major earner of export dollars for the Canadian economy. We all hear a lot about the deficit which we have in our balance of payments. That simply means that we as a country buy or import more than we sell, but the one bright spot in that picture is agriculture. We enjoy a very high standard of living in Canada as a result of an efficient agricultural industry. Not only are we productive enough to do
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
that at home, but we are also productive enough to export a lot of Canadian agricultural products that earn us foreign dollars. We export in the neighbourhood of $7 million to $8 million worth of agricultural products.
We all know that we cannot grow oranges or bananas in this country. It means, therefore, that we must import a lot of fresh fruit and vegetables that are out of season from the southern United States and other countries around the world. There is a big minus, then as far as the agricultural side of our balance of payments is concerned. So if we subtract that from all the things we export and sell to other countries, it still means we have a net surplus as far as agricultural products are concerned to the tune of $3 billion or $4 billion. The agricultural side of our economy is very important, therefore, in terms of having a healthy balance of payments. It is a healthier situation in which to find ourselves when we can sell things to earn foreign dollars rather than simply to raise interest rates in order to attract borrowed dollars into the country. That should be obvious to everyone, in the sense that if you sell things, you earn that money which you do not have to replay; whereas if you borrow money, not only do you have to repay it, but you have to pay interest on it until the debt is finally cleared.
Agriculture is very important to Canada as a trading nation, and we are very much of a trading nation. We have a small country in terms of population but a very large one geographically, and a rich country in terms of natural resources. Having said that, 1 must point out that agriculture is facing some very serious problems in Canada today as a result of what is commonly referred to as the cost-price squeeze. That simply means that our costs in agriculture have been going up drastically. We see increases in energy prices. We see increases in the cost of fertilizer, herbicides and insecticides. We see increases in machinery costs and repairs and virtually everything that goes into a modern farm operation. As I said, a modern farm operation today is different from what it was in the days of my father. For instance, farming has become very capital-intensive and as those costs go up, the farmers have to borrow more money to operate. It then becomes very important in any farmer's budget what kind of interest costs he is going to incur. We are hit in agriculture, Mr. Speaker, with a double whammy effect when our costs go up, because not only do direct costs go up but, in terms of the way farmers finance today, the cost of borrowing money when interest rates go up, and that is what this bill seeks to address at least partly, this evening.
To be fair about it, I think the Government has recognized the fact that there are some problems in the agricultural industry and it has attempted to address some of them in Bill C-134 but this bill addresses a very small sector of the agricultural economy. It is designed to lower interest rates by as much as 4 per cent to those people who have financial problems, in conjunction with a Farm Credit Corpoation loan. And though we give the Government credit for recognizing that there are some problems in agriculture, you have to really question the total understanding of the Government as it relates to the very

November 4, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
large problem which the agricultural industry finds itself in as a result of the high interest rates, and the cost-price squeeze.
Let me refer now to the price side. We have seen major declines in world grain prices and world grain prices of rape-seed, for instance, which has come to be known as canola. We have seen major declines in barley and wheat prices. So at the same time that we are experiencing in agriculture very large increases in costs, we are also experiencing a large drop in grain prices. We can talk all we want, as the Parliamentary Secretary did prior to five o'clock, as to how important it is to have supply management and those kinds of things in place that help the farmer to obtain a better price for his product, but I do not know how he is going to address that problem when it gets to the major earner of export dollars in this country as far as agriculture is concerned, that is, the grain industry. Canada consumes about 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the wheat it grows. Therefore, it has to export the remaining three-quarters, and it would be virtually impossible for Canada to do very much about the world grain price. We know they are very low. Having said that it would be very difficult for the Government to do a lot. I have to point out that there are some things it could be doing that it is not doing. In the last year I had the opportunity to visit with American legislators and to talk with them specifically about what our two grain exporting countries can do to bring about some kind of working arrangement on steadying world grain prices production. We have reported our findings to the Minister of State responsible for the Wheat Board in the other place. 1 have had discussions with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), and nothing has happened.
We know from our discussions with the American Legislators that they are having the same problems expressed to them as are being expressed to those of us here who were elected from agricultural areas of the country. There is a communality of interest there. The American administration is of a slightly different opinion; it is more inclined to go along with the world market situation and not try to interfere in terms of helping to influence prices in the right way. However, I see no reason why the Canadian Government does not see fit to carry on those discussions between the two legislative bodies on both sides of the border. If the Parliamentary Secretary who spoke just before five is really serious in what he said, I hope he will use his influence on the Cabinet Members to see that some discussions take place on which might bring about some of the things he has spoken of. The Opposition is sometimes accused of doing nothing else but talk, but when you are in Government and you have a chance to do something, it seems to me you should do something more than just get up and talk. And I have given the Hon. Member an example.
There are other things I think the Government could be doing to bring about solutions to the farm income problem which is at the root of the Bill we have in front of us this everning, Mr. Speaker. We have heard this afternoon references made to some of the things we as a Party have advocated, such as the agribond concept. The Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) referred to some specific
things which the Americans are doing, such as the establishment to production credit associations, bankers acceptance financing and the setting up of local banks having to do specifically with agriculture and of some federal land banks. These four specific programs are in effect in the U.S., some of them since the 1930s, specifically to aid agriculture in order that American farmers can have access to lower than the going rate of interest.
We on this side are not saying this is going to bring about an immediate solution and solve all our problems, but we are saying there are some things we can be looking at with an eye to solving some of those problems down the road. I have asked questions in this House of the former minister of Finance and of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and I wrote letters to them suggesting that they look at some of the things the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin mentioned this afternoon, but we have been absolutely stonewalled as far as answers are concerned. We are not saying that we think these programs can be simply transferred from one side of the border to the other, that they would work as well here as they apparently have in the U.S. They have worked there, and I will tell you why. There is evidence that the American farmer has access to financing as much as 3 per cent or 4 per cent below that available to Canadian farmers. That to me is evidence that some of those programs have worked, and they have worked over a long period of time. We will never have a chance to see how those programs work here if we do not make some kind of effort at least to try some of them.
We talk about the agribond concept, Mr. Speaker. The former distinguished minister of Agriculture from my party spoke this afternoon about the Lortie Commission and lamented the fact that the so-called blue chip committee set up to look at financing as far as the housing industry is concerned, did not contain-and I think he was accurate-one single person with very much expertise in or exposure to the agricultural side of our economy. However, they came back and recommended that the Government in fact not proceed with some of the financial assistance it was planning for the housing industry.
Even if we cannot do some of those things with respect to the agribond concept, it seems to me that the least it could do is to see that when the Farm Credit Corporation goes to the market it at least gives Canadians a chance to invest in their own country. About two months ago we saw the Farm Credit Corporation going to the American market to raise $100 million to finance Canadian farmers. Now, statistics tell us the Canadian consumer is saving at roughly twice the rate of the American consumer. So I fail to understand why the Government does not have the courage or the courtesy to give Canadians a chance to invest in the most basic industry Canada has, namely, agriculture. I think it is absolutely deplorable that the Farm Credit Corporation, set up by this Government and this Parliament, should go outside the country to raise funds to finance Canadian farmers when we in fact have a tremendous pool of capital here available for investment. So when we talk
November 4, 1982

about investing outside the country, I think this Government should have its knuckles rapped severely for not giving Canadians a chance to invest in Canada. I do not think there can be much of an excuse for that deplorable situation.
I would like to talk now, Mr. Speaker, about some of the additional steps this Government could take doing to assist farmers in terms of income. I happen to have been here at 12.30 this morning, Mr. Speaker, when Royal Assent was given to the Bill to end the work stoppage on the west coast. For every day that strike went on, the Canadian farming community alone lost-by "lost" 1 mean it cannot be regained-something like $8 million in export sales every day. We knew from the outset that the parties involved were probably not going to come back unless they were legislated back. So on that basis I find it deplorable that this Government waited so long to act. If the Government was serious in its concern, not only about the farming community in this country but about the total economy, I fail to see why it did not act much sooner.
In addition to that, several Members on this side have suggested that the Government take a very hard look at the amount of tax it collects on energy used by Canadian farmers in order to stay in production. I have a table in front of me which gives a breakdown of the pump price of gasoline right across the country. Speaking of my own Province of Manitoba, the Federal Government collects roughly 60 cents a gallon in tax. That is the federal charge on each gallon of gasoline consumed in Manitoba, whether it goes into agriculture, recreation or industry. What we have suggested is that the federal Government look at removing part of the 60 cent per gallon tax levied in 1975 and subsequently changed. Removing that tax would immediately have the effect of lowering some of the input costs of Canadian agriculture. This applies not only to farm fuels, because it would have a spin-off effect. We know that a very large component of fertilizer, of insecticides and pesticides, many of the things farmers need to be productive today, cost more as a result of that 1.5 cent a litre tax. The Government has refused to look at that. Well, even if it does not want to look at it, surely it should be willing to change the way it is administered. What the Government does in the case of agriculture is to collect that 1.5 cents a litre and then refund it under certain circumstances. In the case of the farming community, it is refunded if it is used on the farm for agricultural production. The farmer has to pay the tax and then apply for a refund. We all know that, theoretically, it should not make any difference; if you pay something one day and you get it back the next, it should not make a lot of difference. But what happens in many cases is that the farmer pays the tax, and it takes anywhere from two months to two years before the farmer gets aroung to doing his book work and applies for the refund. In the case of Manitoba it is actually illegal to use fuel on a farm other than the fuel eligible for the tax refund.
So I have suggested in Committee, and to several of the Ministers opposite, that they consider not even collecting the
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
tax. That would at least give the farmer a break in his immediate cash outlay, and that does not seem to me to be unreasonable. It would also save some administration costs. It seems ludicrous to me that the Government should have to incur the administration costs that it does to collect the tax and then turn around and refund it when there is a way, as there is in Manitoba with which I am very familiar, of not collecting the tax in the first place. Now, there is something very simple and straightforward which would simplify the paper work, that is, get rid of some of the bureaucracy of which we all think we have too much. And yet this Government does not even want to look at it. That is another example of some of the things the Government could do.
Another thing it could do to help farmers get by without borrowing any more money than they have to is to sit down and talk with the banks to see if the banks would be willing to go along with some fixed term financing for specific projects. The farmer could go into the bank in the spring and know he was going to pay a fixed rate of interest rather than a floating rate over the production period, whether it be for feeding cattle for six months or growing a crop which may take six or eight months from the time it is sown. If the farmer knew that the financing he was obtaining for a specific enterprise was going to be fixed over a period of time, it would mean he could do a much better job of budgeting. It works both ways. Two or three years ago that looked great because prices of everything went up over the production period. If you borrowed money in the spring of 1980 at 11 per cent or 12 per cent, in the fall you paid 3 per cent or 4 per cent more. As was pointed out again by the Parliamentary Secretary earlier today, over the last 12 or 13 weeks interest rates have come down, and we all welcome that. But it means that in this particular year the person who borrowed at a fixed rate will be caught. Fixed term financing at least would eliminate one of the variables as far as production costs for that particular farming enterprise is concerned. This is something at which they could look. It has been suggested many times to the Government.
Let me talk about the general taxation level in the country, but first let me indicate how this topic relates to the Bill at hand. One of the reasons farmers borrow money is to buy land. We all know that one of the big costs associated with purchasing land is the additional costs which farmers incur because they have to pay capital gains taxes. If there were some recognition of the problem this was causing, it would mean that the farming community would get by with less borrowing. It could transfer land from one generation to the other, from father to son, while borrowing less money.
We moved on that when we were the Government. We included a basic exemption for capital gains and a commitment in the budget, which was defeated in December, 1979, to look at the entire question of capital gains. The Liberal Party, at its convention in the early summer of 1980, promised to look at it, but it has not happened.

November 4, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
As agriculture becomes more and more capital intensive, this will become a major factor in the ability of Canadian agriculture to be as productive and as competitive with agricultural sectors in other countries around the world. Let me indicate why. As 1 said at the opening of my remarks, agriculture is a very productive industry. It is productive because it has become very capital intensive, but I submit that it is the only major industry in Canada which has to regenerate its capital, pay for itself and pay for the land every time there is a new generation of farmers on the land. We know the stock market has been rising astronomically to record levels in the last two or three days. This does not mean that the people operating Union Carbide or Canadian Pacific have to put up more money when stocks rise in order to stay in business. They do not own the stocks. Their ownership is divided widely across the country. Anyone can purchase shares in these companies, if they have the money. The equity in these companies is shared widely across the entire base of the Canadian economy or the American economy, but when we turn to agriculture, that is not the case.
Every farmer tries-and so far has been reasonably successful-to pay for and own their farms. A major issue which 1 believe will have to be dealt with very quickly is the fact that every time a new generation goes on to another piece of land, it means that the land has to earn enough money for the farmer to pay for it over his lifetime. If a farmer, as was the case in the past, thinks of the ownership of his land and a retirement fund so that he can live out his golden years or his retirement years in some kind of dignity, it means that he must sell the land to someone else to obtain his retirement income. If he sells a parcel of land and obtains some money, he has to pay a big chunk of it in capital gains. This means that the person buying the land is required to pay more than he would without these very onerous rates of capital gains.
Unless we address this issue, we will find that the only people owning land in the country, very shortly, will be the Government. 1 find this fact very disturbing, especially when the country was settled not more than two or three generations ago by people who came here with the prospect of owning their land.
In not much more than a hundred years that prospect has been taken away. Young people who are starting to farm now-and I know this for a fact; I can cite various examples from across the Prairies and I suspect the same is true in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes-have to rent land and do not have the prospect of ever owning their land as did their fathers. If we get into a situation where we do not have family farms, which are the basis of Canadian agricultural productivity, we will not be as productive agriculturally and the entire country will suffer.
The Government should address the problem of capital gains if it is serious about doing something for agriculture. I do not want to belabour the point any more than I have to, but 1 find it absolutely incredible that the Minister of Agriculture,
who has been in his job for something like ten years, can rise- and I have read most of his speeches-and talk about the problems in agriculture but not offer a solution except for the bill before us. He travels and delivers as many speeches as any Member of Cabinet.
As I have said, we are pleased that the Government has recognized the problems. There are something in the order of
150,000	grain farmers in the three western Provinces, yet this Bill provides only $16 million for interest rebates. This amounts to $10 per farmer, if that amount is divided among only the grain farmers of western Canada.
The other side of the equation is that we in Canadian agriculture are not looking for handouts. We want to pay our way. We are proud. We have always done it in the past and we will do it again if we are given a chance, but we need some Government support. We need Government support when we go to GATT. We need a government to go to bat for us, so that when members of the Canadian agricultural community go to sell to other countries around the world they do so on a fair basis.
I could cite several examples. We have the most eminent authority on the Canadian beef industry present in the Chamber this evening, the Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave). He could literally speak for hours on the failings of the Government, how it has not properly represented the beef industry and has not given it a fair chance to trade with other countries around the world. These are some of the things which we should legitimately expect from the federal Government, if it cared about what 1 believe to be the most basic industry in Canada.
Let me conclude on a note of optimism. I believe farmers are the most resourceful and productive members of the Canadian economy. I may sound as if I were blowing my own horn, since I represent an agricultural constituency and I have farmed all my life. I am proud to be a farmer; I am a farmer by choice. It will take more than the present Government and more than the Minister of Agriculture to run Canadian agriculture into the ground. Canadian farmers have more land per capita than any other farmer in the world. We have some of the most productive land in the world. We will succeed. If we have a change of Government, we will have a federal minister of Agriculture who will understand the basic problems. In that event things will be done for farmers. We will not have to pass Mickey Mouse bills in the House, such as the one before us this evening. Again the industry will be able to finance itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course, the point of order just raised by my colleague for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) is not a point of order at all, but simply a way of making a comment. In any event, Mr. Speaker, we are considering this evening Bill C-134 which follows from the budget brought down on June 28, 1982, by the then Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
It gives me great pleasure to speak about this bill this evening, especially since some of my colleagues and I accompanied today the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to the International Agricultural Fair in Montreal which will go on until November 7. When we look at the farming community and agricultural organizations and realize that many people are becoming more and more involved in this industry, it is gratifying to note that Canadian agriculture has become much more sophisticated, and diversified, and I can speak from experience, Mr. Speaker, since I come from a rural municipality where my father is still a farmer. I can tell this House that, as far as Canadian agriculture is concerned, unlike the previous speaker who advocates a change of Government and of Minister, the Canadian farmers must admit today that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who has held his portfolio for ten years, had done more than any of his predecessors for Canadian agriculture. He has made it progressive, competitive and productive, so that agricultural producers now own small, medium-size and even large businesses. However, what I want to say about this bill this evening after my visit this morning with the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, and my colleagues, the Hon. Members for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) and for Beauce (Mr. Lapointe), to the International Fair, is that, in my opinion, because of the present economic situation, while the farmers work very hard to succeed in their business like any other businessman in Canada, it is quite obvious that they have had to face higher interest rates, which has thrown their budget out of balance, even though interest rates are now going down. We all hope that this downward trend will continue, but we have to face the facts and realize that the figures show that we now have in Canada and in Quebec a great many middle-aged farmers, farmers over 40 years old or perhaps as young as 35, who have had to invest in their farms for several years.
Farmers who, like many businesses, are long established, have raised loans at lower interest rates than the prevailing rates and can face the competition and cope with present conditions much more easily. However, we now have young farmers or farmers who, even if they cannot necessarily be called young, have only been established on a farm for a few years, and they have had to make huge investments, not only on a monetary level, but also on the human level and for equipment, and they have what could be described as relatively
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
large debts. Consequently, to maintain their productivity and their financial position, they have to work increasingly hard to make both ends meet. They are not the only ones in that situation, Mr. Speaker.
I believe that many Canadians in most of our businesses must now reassess their productivity and financial position and try to work differently and to be perhaps more conscientious. However, in addition to the situation of farmers and of businessmen who must reassess their productivity and financial position, there were many farmers who were only starting in agriculture or who had only a few years behind them and who have had to borrow money quite recently, but the interest rates offered by the Farm Credit Corporation at that time and the increases they had to face have caused them hardship. Many farmers from Quebec and other parts of Canada attending the International Farm Exhibition in Montreal had the opportunity today to meet their elected representatives. Referring to my own province, the Hon. Members for Quebec, made representations concerning the Farm Credit Corporation's high interest rates claiming in these hard times they could not cope with the financial burden they had assumed in borrowing from the Farm Credit Corporation or would have to assume now if they borrowed from the Corporation. Consequently the Quebec Members have appealed to the Government, the Cabinet and more specifically the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the hope he would pursue the efforts he has been making ever since he was appointed minister a decade ago, to help farmers survive this temporary high interest rate situation. On the basis of these recommendations, on June 28 1982, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) came up with this section in the budget documents:
Special Farm Financial Assistance Program
And I quote from the first two paragraphs on page 25, Mr. Speaker:
The government is introducing a new assistance program for farmers to be delivered through the Farm Credit Corporation.
Over the next two years loans totalling $200 million will be made under the program to farmers in Financial distress. The loans will be made at the regular FCC interest rate-
-which was at the time, in June, 16'/2 per cent, and is now 15% per cent-
-but a rebate of 4 percentage points will be provided for the first two years of the loan. The Government is allocating $100 million to the program ($84 million as a special contribution to the FCC for lending to farmers and $16 million to pay for the interest rebates) and the FCC will divert $116 million to the program from its regular lending fund.
The program was to be implemented immediately, but it had to be completely by an act to amend the provisions of the Farm Credit Act. The important point is that many Canadians interested in agriculture are asking themselves important questions the investments and purchases farmers make and at times wonder how they can balance their budgets. But I suggest that although agriculture is still agriculture, it can

November 4, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
aptly be referred to as industrial agriculture while and farmers may be regarded as manufacturers. They have certainly something in common: investments. A manufacturer may invest his money into a plant 200 x 200 which together with its buildings and machinery, appears less impressive to the eye than a farm with its buildings, machinery and appliances which, because of the very nature of the various crops, may be used only a few months, weeks, or even days each year.
But the situation is not the same for a farmer during the haying season: he must have the implements required for that kind of work even though they will remain idle once the work is completed. Things are different in the manufacturing sector; if you have a press-I see that my colleague from Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) agrees with me-to do some printing or if you are in the furniture-making industry, your equipment can be used all year round, and as my colleague from Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) points out-I see that my colleague from Verdun-Saint-Paul (Mr. Savard), the new Government deputy whip is also in agreement-the farmer uses his implements for a few days only whereas people in the industrial sector use theirs all year long. With respect to depreciation, some of those investments must be taken into consideration and, when it comes to the investments which farmers have to make, they can sometimes be looked upon from a different perspective. I could give a number of examples of machinery which is used only periodically but which may very well cost as much if not more than equipment found in manufacturing plants.
As to whether or not they should share that depreciation, they must indeed do it on their own or pay it off in a different way. So, once this special financial assistance program was announced by the Canadian Government on June 28, it was imperative that we should be able to tell Canadians in our ridings just how important the agricultural sector is. It is important to keep in mind the fact that all the food we find on our tables is produced by the agricultural sector and that if the farmers who grow our food can indeed produce and compete, consumers will be better off. That is why we have to challenge those who keep saying that farmers get a lot more help than other organizations or other businesses.
Mr. Speaker, 1 think we may have been misled by people who make such statements, because any commercial or manufacturing business can benefit from tax exemptions or lower interest rates, or again get help through grants, but the situation is not necessarily the same in agriculture. All things considered in light of this Bill, the Canadian Government was quite justified in launching that program. I should mention as well the program for small businesses and fishermen described on page 10 of the June budget.
Perhaps we could look at the situation covered by Bill C-134. At this point, Mr. Speaker, if we consider investment and the amount of money farmers must invest, it would be useful
to know the maximum amount now available under the Farm Credit Act. Since the legislation has been adapted to the economic, industrial and social requirements of agriculture today, loans to up to $300,000 per qualified applicant and as high as $500,000 for a group. The interest rate is calculated in terms of the return on Government treasury bills, plus 1 per cent, over a period of from five to ten years.
Mr. Speaker, the Farm Credit Corporation, through the Farm Credit Act, provides opportunities for financial assistance of up to $300,000 per individual and $500,000 per group, because the Canadian government realizes that our agriculture has made constant progress, and that even if they have a certain amount of money in the bank, farmers should have the same loan facilities as manufacturers and businessmen. Twenty years ago, Mr. Speaker, we had a situation where manufacturers could borrow on the equity in their companies, while the farm situation was quite different from today, when we see that farm capital has increased at an astonishing rate during the last few years, unlike the more gradual progression in the manufacturing sector, so that there have been considerable changes in the agricultural sector. Therefore, the Farm Credit Act has been an excellent instrument for showing Canadians and Canadian farmers that governments were well aware of the progress and productivity on our farms, and that it was necessary to find mechanisms and funding to meet their requirements. And this is what happened under the Farm Credit Act when loan ceilings were raised.
However, if we consider Bill C-134, to continue what I was saying at the beginning, namely that recently, people had borrowed at interest rates which normally would have allowed them to function, we had to realize that the sharp rise in interest rates was upsetting the financial forecasts made by FCC advisers and agronomists who are increasingly involved in counselling farmers, and in fact they have always done so, but let us say that the process is now so refined that every young farmer or farm producer has access to professional help, as in many other organizations, and it was normal that that should be case in farming.
As I was saying, since projections had been made, it became necessary following representations that had been made to deal with the matter and this was done through the Bill now under consideration which is providing a 4 per cent rebate on a two-year basis for interest rates. Of course, the Opposition will suggest that it is not enough. 1 think Mr. Speaker, when substantial funds of $100 million are allotted to the Corporation, it means that the Government of Canada recognizes the importance of agriculture in this country. It is essential through those budgets to make Canadians realize that the production of food is quite important and that the funds allotted to farming should be directly proportionate to productivity, to the farmer's holdings and fixed assets. I think that it is a rather important matter. This 4 per cent rebate has been granted following projections made by various farming experts
November 4, 1982

of the Farm Credit Corporation, by personal counsellors or by other agricultural accounting advisers. The anticipated increase of interest rates having unbalanced their budget such a relevant legislation was necessary because for several months now, the inflation rate having decreased both in Canada and in the United States, interest rates have been dropping.
1 think this is the result of the policy put forward by the Government in his fight against inflation and even recently when the new Minister of Finance delivered his financial statement, inflation being momentarily reduced, we saw the Government of Canada extend for a 2 year period that 4 per cent rebate hoping, and being increasingly convinced that since the inflation rate as well as interest rates are considerably lower this will allow farmers to do some planning but if indeed interest rates are really different in months or years ahead the Farm Credit Corporation will readjust them as it did some time ago when it brought its interest rates down from 16.5 to 15.75 per cent. We needed some sort of a mechanism to respond adequately to those well-justified representations and this is why we are dealing with this Bill. I heard the previous speaker say that it was a fine Bill but of course he would never admit that it is an excellent one. I hope that we will soon refer the whole matter to the Standing Committee on Agriculture if not to the committee of the House for immediate consideration through all stages to speed up the process because a larger number of questions directed to the Minister of Agriculture before June 28, 1982 actually had to do with interest rates.
1 trust that my colleagues opposite will pass this legislation without delay because they were asking the Minister of Agriculture many questions requesting a reduction in interest rates or some interest related assistance. I do hope that after listening to the previous speaker, who says he is closely involved with the farmers, and I know that for a fact his colleagues will be convinced to pass this legislation without delay. I think it is important as well, to read Clause 3 of the bill and in particular subclause 3(4), and I quote:
Where an amount may be paid to an eligible farmer pursuant to subsection (1) in relation to a loan payment period, the Minister shall, where it is practicable to do so, make such payment in the loan payment period to which the payment relates.
And subclause 3 states as well and I quote:
Where, in or before any loan payment period in relation to which an eligible farmer may be paid pursuant to subsection (1), the eligible farmer
(a)	ceases to be a farmer, or
(b)	ceases to follow the plan of farming operations submitted by him to the
Corporation,
before he has been paid pursuant to subsection (1), no payments shall be made to him pursuant to that subsection in relation to that or any following loan payment period.
How should this provision be interpreted? What is important, is to tell the Canadian people that if at any given time, representations were made to the effect that we were helping farmers too much and that after getting a loan or some
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
financial assistance, farmers would quit their operation, and that therefore the Canadian government would have invested money unduly. Well, we have now a provision stating that in such cases no payment will be made or the loan will be called and the operator will lose all his rights in this regard. 1 think such a provision was important to avoid useless loans or assistance being given out as has happened in the past in the manufacturing sector or other similar industries.
It is often said that unfortunately, when a business asks for a government loan or any kind of government assistance it will have less difficulty getting it because you deal with the government, which is less careful about it. 1 think that governments and . .. this Government in particular have nevertheless made sure that farmers who do receive a loan will use it for the right purposes, as would any lending institution do, whether a bank or a "caisse populaire."
Mr. Speaker, when we look at the situation of the young Canadian farmers in particular we can readily see that it was important to tell them they would get assistance if they really wanted to remain in agriculture, whether as a dairy farmer or a livestock operator. I think this message was very important and was well understood from this side of the House, given the representations that were made to Hon. Members, as far as the Province of Quebec is concerned, by organizations such as the UPA, the Cooperative federee as well as millers, who were asking for financial assistance so that this economic sector may operate according to acceptable standards consistent with those that may exist in other industrial or business areas. And 1 believe they were representations. Farmers did not ask for charity, all they wanted given the present situation, is to be allowed to continue their operations so that our Canadian agro-food industry may successfully compete and production be maintained at the level we have known for several years. I think it was a very impotant message and the response, that is Bill C-134, is equally important. When a farmer is temporarily in dire straits, 1 believe we must take action, and this has been well understood, as I was saying a moment ago, on this side of the House. So, Mr. Speaker, given this situation-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in participating in the debate on Bill C-134, an Act to amend the Farm Credit Act in Canada. I would just like to make a few comments. We do take pleasure in participating in the debate but, as the Hon. Member on the Government side pointed out just a few moments ago, the budget which brought this Bill forward was announced on June 28, some four months ago. The Hon. Member on the Government side is now urging us to pass it immediately. As a matter of fact he is in such a rush that he took about 40 minutes to urge us to pass it immediately.
Those of us on this side have a few things to say about the Bill. We all recognize the problems which are prevalent in agriculture. Sometimes I think that those of us on this side may be a little more aware of the problems than the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is sometimes, and some though not all the Hon. Members of his Party. That would even include the Parliamentary Secretary who may occasionally be a little more aware than the Minister.
This Bill applies only to farmers who are in financial distress. It is designed for farmers who find themselves in need of refinancing. It does not meet many of the needs of the agricultural sector in Canada, and it definitely does not meet too many of the needs of the agricultural sector in the part of the country that I come from. This is not the first time we have seen this Program, Mr. Speaker. The November budget announced a $50 million Program for Special Financial Farm Assistance loans. That $50 million helped 382 farmers in Canada-not in one Province, not in one country, but in the whole of the country. An additional $100 million was provided for special farm financing in the June budget, but $116 million was taken away from Farm Credit general funds and applied to this Program. That meant that someone who had the ability and wished to farm was probably going to be denied the opportunity because there was insufficient funding. This $116 million was not additional money. The Government used the jiggery-pockery it indulges in quite often. It took the $116 million and said, "Now we have a $216 million Program". Things do not work out quite like, that, Mr. Speaker.
Even though the cost of money is coming down, financing is a leading input cost in the farming sector in Canada. It accounts for about 20 per cent of the total cost of production. The future is not that bright for farmers at the moment, Mr. Speaker. There are projections of a 20 per cent decline in net farm income. It is expected that farmers will receive about $3.4 billion less for their production in 1982 than they did in 1981.
Even those Members who do not have the privilege of representing an agricultural area recognize the importance of agriculture to our economy. One-sixth of all economic activity in Canada is generated in the agrifood business, and a large amount of our balance of trade can be directly attributed to the agriculture industry.
In 1981 we exported $8.8 billion worth of agricultural products and imported $5.6 billion worth of food products. Canada has the ability to bring that figure down to zero. If the programs were in place, the farm population, with its ability, intelligence and skills, would ensure that we do not import farm products at any time.
In the last year, western farmers produced 42 million tonnes of grain. That includes 24 million tonnes of wheat. Canada is the second largest exporter of grain in the world. This year, our grain export business will be worth $6.4 billion.
Fast evening we went through a very difficult exercise, passing a Bill to ensure that the strike at the ports which shut down the whole west coast of Canada could be resolved and the grain worth $6.4 billion could be shipped and bring badly needed money into the country.
People engaged in agriculture need programs that will help them and allow them to use their abilities and their skills- their raw, gut, "stick-to-itiveness" and toughness. If such programs were in place, we would not need a 4 per cent reduction in the cost of money. If the Government removed some of the stumbling blocks that hinder the agricultural community, we would not even have to consider this Bill.
The strike of the last 16 days has cost $8 million per day in lost grain exports. Those exports were lost, Mr. Speaker, and not deferred as the assistant to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in the other place has said. He claimed that those sales were deferred; Mr. Speaker, the sales were lost. Over $120 million was lost to the Canadian economy because of the work stoppage on the west coast. If it were the case that we were going to stop growing or exporting grain on July 31, then it could be claimed that the sales were deferred. But we are going to continue growing grain and continue stretching our rail transportation system and continue exporting forever. So that $8 million per day was lost, Mr. Speaker.
1 cannot understand the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Speaker. Before the session was resumed on October 27 he was claiming that one of the first orders of business would be to use the force of Parliament to resolve the work stoppage on the west coast. Action was delayed until the Monday following resumption, then until Tuesday and finally till Wednesday; a delay of seven days.
Earlier in the House I heard the Hon. Member for Hum-boldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) speak about the great concern that Members of the New Democratic Party have for the grain producers and farmers. He spoke of what that Party would like to do for the farmers. But last night every Member of that Party who was present voted against the resolution of the work stoppage. The Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Fake (Mr. Anguish) voted against it, although it
November 4, 1982

caused him a great deal of anguish-and that is not a play on words. The Elon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, the Hon. Member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky), the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant), all those who were present, voted for continuation of the work stoppage.
I do not understand that, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps I should. Even though the people of western Canada sent the majority of the Members of the New Democratic Party to this House, control of those Members has passed from the people in that part of Canada. It has been placed in the hands of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) or the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). Not a Member from the rural areas of Saskatchewan or Manitoba spoke for his constituents in the House last night. That was evident in the way they voted. There is something to be said for those Members who were absent. The Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) spoke in my part of Canada saying that we have to get the grain moving, because that is important. He was not in the House yesterday, however. Perhaps if he had been, he would have suffered the torment that some of the other Members of that Party did when obeying the Party line. So he was absent.
When we looked at the Government's attempt, through an amendment, we asked them to have a second look and, take six and five out. It was meant for the Public Service, but now it will be applied in all likelihood to the private sector, the private economy of Canada. That is something I am sure the Members of the Government and the New Democratic Party will not be allowed to forget.
Looking at priorities, I mentioned earlier that if the Government would remove some of the stumbling blocks, the huge obstacles they place in front of the agricultural community, we would not need a 4 per cent reduction in interest. As my learned colleague, the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out earlier, the men and women of the farming community of Canada do not want a handout, they do not ask for a subsidy. What they ask for is a fair chance to produce. They want to use their God-given skills and the soil they have been given to feed a hungry world. They do not want subsidies, unless Government programs make it necessary for them to ask for assistance. That is the only time you hear their cry.
A prime example is the fuel tax on agriculture. When I went back to the farm in 1965, my fuel costs were negligible. They were less then for a whole season's operation than they are now for one month. If the Government tax on agricultural fuel were removed, the producers of agricultural products in Canada would be much better off. We hear there will be another $4 per barrel increase in the spring, a furthur tax on the production of food to be used to feed a hungry world.
As the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) and the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) mentioned, if capital gains were removed, the need for a farmer to ask for a larger sum of money for his land would be reduced. The
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
capital required would be reduced and there would be more Farm Credit funds.
I know you understand, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister is well aware that the farmer may pass his land to his or her children. That is understandable. It is as it should be. However, I have seen two examples in the last three months in my office involving a son who had inherited his father's land while his mother was still living, and the son having died tragically, left the land to his mother. Capital gains applied to the transfer of that land. I cannot understand a Minister of Finance or a Government being so hungry for money, so greedy that when a son or daughter dies and leaves the land to a mother or father they want to tax it. It does not make sense. It is another obstacle in the way of production, another roadblock for the agricultural producers of this country. If that were removed, we would not have to talk about a 4 per cent rebate over two years. In the farming community, two years is not considered a long-term program. I have here a pamphlet from the 1979 election wherein the Minister of Agriculture promised to bring the valuation day of farmland up to 1974. Also, I have a copy of a speech he made where he stated that if the Liberal Party was re-elected, the tax on agricultural fuel would be removed. We have not seen that.
When questioned in the House by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), the Minister said that was not policy, it was a promise made in the heat of debate. He was saying, "We will put it down. We will make statements in a handout that is distributed door to door, but it is in the heat of debate, don't expect it folks, don't really believe what 1 tell you." He does not have to say that because a lot of people in Canada are beginning to think that way without prompting.
We have had some bills, proposals through Farm Credit and a few other things from this Minister of Agriculture to which I would like to draw attention. They are programs which relate so supply management not requested by the agricultural community. If the agricultural community as a whole requests a board and is represented on or controls that board, there is nothing wrong with that. However, let me very quickly compare North America to the U.S.S.R.
In 1970, both the United States and the U.S.S.R. exported grain. The United States exported 38 million tonnes and the Russians exported eight million tonnes. In 1981 the Americans were exporting 115 million tonnes and the Russians were importing 43 million tonnes.
We all use seed on our farms. In Russia they take 16 per cent of their harvest for seed. In North America we take 2 per cent of our harvest to put back in the ground. It is a funny thing. The latest thing on Government controls, Government intervention in the marketplace and in the agricultural community is in Russia. Right now, in November 1982, they know how much fertilizer they are going to put in the ground in the spring of 1984 because it is in the 1981-1985 five-year plan. On my farm and on those of my colleagues, that decision will be made in the spring of 1984 after we have the soil tested, looked at the weather and checked the markets. That is when we will make the decision about the fertilizer.
