One of the reasons why the U.S.S.R. is now one of the world's largest importers, not only of grains but of meat, is Government intervention. Even the Minister of Agriculture recognizes that. In western Canada the Minister stated that we should be thankful that the U.S.S.R. is Communist, because if they were not, we would not be able to sell them the food we grow. In other words, they would grow enough themselves if they changed their system of government.
I would like to speak for a moment on the cost to producers. The Government's program regarding the statutory movement of grain will cost the producers a lot of money. I say to people in any part of Canada who are concerned and think there may be some hope in the 74 members of the Liberal Government Party voting against that measure that that will be the frosty Friday. I have yet to see Members of the Government Party, let alone Cabinet Ministers, vote against a Government bill. If there is hope in western Canada that the Liberal Party will help to stop the change or somehow modify the change in the Crow rate or have any input directed to that, I say to my friends in the west that that will not happen.
In conclusion I want to say a few words about the economy of Canada. We heard of megaprojects which were cancelled by this Government, Alsands, Cold Lake, all of them put on hold. In my Province alone, Mr. Speaker, there is a megaproject every spring, and that project is worth a billion dollars to the men and women in the agricultural community. Every spring there is a renewable megaproject. A billion dollars goes into the ground. That is a megaproject, Mr. Speaker, to which this Government should pay a little more attention, not a megaproject of $2 billion for only a year. This is $1 billion. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister agreeing. That is a megaproject, a billion dollars a year put in by the men and women in my Province who are involved in the agricultural community. That project would be much better served if the policies of the Government opposite were directed more toward allowing the men and women to function, to go ahead without the interference, without the capital gains, without the farm fuel tax, without these things that get in the way. We need bills that give us a 4 per cent rebate over two years for farmers in financial distress, and that probably would involve less than 700 farms in all of Canada involved in this Program.
As many faults as I can find with the Program, Mr. Speaker, it appears to be the best this Government can put forward, and I will support it because I cannot expect any more.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am pleased to speak on Bill C-134, an Act respecting rebates of interest on farm loans made under the Farm Credit Act. I would like to start off my remarks by stating we feel it is another band-aid solution to a very important, vital question in Canada with regard to one of our major industries, the farming industry, across Canada.
1 want to refer, if I may, to the remarks made by the Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson). The Parliamentary Secretary indicated he had been in the farming industry for 45 years, but he seemed to brush over the fact of these farm bankruptcies in Canada. They were not really that significant and we did not have too much to worry about. I want to say to that Hon. Member that in the farming industry, farmers do not come about just by one or two days' experience. They come up through generations, through family tradition, and their experience whether it is that of one farmer or several
November 4, 1982

farmers, is something we cannot afford to lose. We are losing the expertise, the professional people in those areas. I travelled on the Transport Committee of 1980 across the prairies. The groups that came to us, the farmers' unions, the grain elevator people, time and time again stressed the problem of the abandonment of rail lines, which this Government has allowed to happen. They are not asking for handouts. They are asking this Government to recognize the fact that when it allows the abandonment of rail lines it is creating an extra hardship for those people who have to bring their grain farther distances to the grain elevators, the ports, or to their transportation system. On top of that, this Government has brought in legislation that adds to that cost. Not only have they lost the rail lines, but now they are paying out additional costs for energy. This Government has to recognize the fact that it is creating hardships that cannot be sustained. These farmers reach out and try to develop or plan, but this kind of help is not going to meet their requirements. I do not think the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex fully understands the kind of problems that this has brought about, even though he may have 45 years of experience and may have developed a plan over that period of time.
Here is what we heard from a group representing a large area, the Peace River area. They talk about the age of farm operators, and the potential for further expansion of farming activities is indicated by a relatively large number of young farmers in the district. They give the average age of farm operators: under 25 years of age, 3.53 per cent; 25 to 44 years of age, almost 46 per cent; 45 to 59 years of age, 36.47 per cent; 60 to 69 years of age, 11.24 per cent, and over 70 years, 2.88. What 1 am trying convey is that we have a lot of young, experienced farmers who are trying to take over from their parents and operate the farms, and they need that financial help. They need a long-term support program so that they can plan ahead. If that money were made available, it would stimulate our manufacturing sectors because they would be able to plan some kind of development.
There is a fertilizer plant in my riding in British Columbia, and this summer the walls were bulging with fertilizer, and everyone knows there is no requirement for fertilizer in June or July. So there were lay-offs at that plant. But would it not make sense to have long-range financing for farmers so that they could purchase their fertilizer in the summer and have it available first thing in the spring? Not only would we be accommodating the farming sector, but this fertilizer plant in British Columbia, and others, would be functioning in an orderly manner as well. That is the kind of economic planning needed, and this Government has to recognize that fact and meet those requirements.
1 want to speak for a moment about CP Rail or the railway system and its abandonments, because I think it is vital to this question. I have not heard the Conservative Party speak too much about the Crow rate or the abandonment of rail lines even though it is vital to what we are talking about. While we see the Government speak about how railways must make a profit, where was the Government when CP Rail was dividing

their corporation? Where was the Government when CP separated its real estate portion into Marathon Realty? What about CP investments? CP Rail has built an empire in this country on the backs of the Canadian people, and this government supports that kind of program. Every time Ian Sinclair comes before the Government, the programs are presented to the House of Commons and in most cases supported by the Liberals and Conservatives. And the farmers and people across Canada have to suffer the consequences.
I want to speak for a moment about a comment made by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight). He outlined a problem with capital gains tax in his riding. He spoke of a father turning a property over to his son, and the son to his mother because of a death, and she had to pay capital gains tax. I want to ask the Members of the Conservative Party of Canada where they were when they were in Government? They were in Government for nine months, and why was that legislation not changed if they feel so strongly about it today? Why, in those nine months when you were in Government, did you not look at this legislation that you are so concerned about and bring it before the House and have it changed? No, they were too busy with other things. In fact, they were elected in late February and did not call the House in for a sitting until October, so that is the kind of concern that that Party had for that kind of legislation.
I would also like to refer to another problem in my riding, the beautiful area of the Creston Valley, a grain and fruit growing area. These people are faced with the closure of the grain elevators. I can understand why they had to make that decision in light of the costs they had been burdened with. Naturally they have to look at running an efficient business, and when the Government creates that kind of burden, who is going to suffer? What happens? They close their grain elevators down. What happens to the expertise of the farmers in those areas? Can you imagine the problems which will be created with regard to storing and shipping their products in an orderly manner?
The Government has made some suggestions, but the problems created are almost devastating. When it comes to the fruit growing industry, another vital part of this riding, the cost of energy involved in transporting products to market is almost unbearable. There are a lot of cattle producers in my area and transportation is very costly. Again, that has been created by the Government, and the Government's programs have done nothing to recognize the needs of farmers in this area. I think it is a sad day when we in Canada cannot recognize that farming is one of our top priority areas. It is an area which could get many other sectors of a given riding rolling again and meeting the requirements, not only of this country but of many other countries as well.
1 would also like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to another of the comments made by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster with regard to the west coast ports dispute. I know farmers across Canada were as concerned as everyone in this Party about that dispute, but I want to say that the farmers

honestly want to treat those workers as fairly as they themselves want to be treated by this Government. It is because of the attitude of this Government toward working people, toward the farming community, toward regional areas, instead of working in a co-operative way, which has created the hardships that the average worker and the average farmer have to face here in Canada. The Hon. Member tried to point to this Party as not having any feelings for the farming community or for the workers in these areas. These workers did not create the problem. 1 must emphasize the fact that it was the employers who had those workers locked out. It was their decision to lock them out and create the problem that the farmers were faced with. So we in this Party have recognized both sides of the problem and 1 think we have dealt with it as responsibly as we could.
This Bill, Mr. Speaker, does not supply the kind of relief needed, and we feel that unless the Government recognizes the serious problems facing the farming community across Canada, we are going to be faced with some very, very serious bankruptcies. The Government has to recognize that in this industry they must have some long-term planning. There must be long-term financing available so that when the farmers are trying to regulate or plan the kinds of production they want to carry out and meet the needs of Canadians, they must be sure that the money will be available at stable interest rates so that they will not have to worry about a fluctuation in their costs of production. They also do not need the threat of a change in the Crow rate hanging over their heads.
Young farmers are not being encouraged to enter into the farming stream and to continue the tradition of earning their livelihoods in an orderly manner. I think the Government is treating problems in the farming community in the same manner as it has treated unemployment or any other problem. It has used a band-aid approach to a very serious problem. The Government should take its head out of the sand and recognize the needs of the farming community. It should bring forth a policy which helps not only the farming community but ail other areas which feed into that system. If it does not do so, indeed there will be very serious problems within the community.
I have already singled out CP Rail. Ian Sinclair comes before the Government, and it dances to his tune. It danced to his tune when it brought in the six and five program, when the rail abandonments took place and when VIA Rail was discussed. The Government took it off its hands, at literally hundreds of millions of dollars of savings to the Company. In fact, the Company charged the Government an extra month's billing on the passenger operation. In other words, it charged its regular fee for the use of its tracks for 12 months, and added a thirteenth month for extra costs.
We sat in on Committee hearings and heard about this. We found that the company had not yet been audited and that some of the audits had not been done for two years. It seems that CP Rail can obtain the required moneys. Also it seems that we are coming into a rail expansion. Goodness knows it is needed to meet the needs of the farming community. It seems
money is available while it is diverting funds, separating various groups away from the railway system and allowing the Government to carry the load in these areas. It is asking the Government to change the Crow agreement while the farming community has to pay the extra load.
There is little enough in the Bill without its creating an additional burden. The farming community cannot stand the changes the Government is anticipating. I believe the Conservative Party should also be putting pressure on the Government to ensure that the Crow rate is not changed and that it is protected in the interests of farming communities across Canada. This is true also in terms of the Atlantic Provinces. We have now discovered that any change in this regard could seriously affect eastern Canada, and that there are other areas which must be taken into consideration now. I say to Liberal Members who represent these areas that they should take a serious look at what is being put forward. There could be serious ramifications on top of what has already been put in place.
These are the types of problems faced by the farming community. We on this side of the House are not happy with this piece of legislation. We see it as a band-aid approach. We have no alternative but to support it, yet the fact remains, as a Member of the Conservative Party pointed out, that it is a Mickey Mouse piece of legislation which will not meet the needs or come anywhere close to helping the Canadian farming community. It will probably carry the load for a few who will qualify, but many will find, when they go to banks or credit unions to obtain money, that no money is available. I have talked with various farmers in my riding. They tell me that it is all very good that the legislation is there, but they ask how and when they can obtain money. They say, "I need it now. I have some planting to do, but there is no money available." What good is this piece of legislation? It is no better than the small business bond.
I had occasion to go into a bank with a small-businessman who was going out of business. I said to the banker, "Here is the legislation; you are supposed to help this man." He said, "I am sorry, but we do not have any money available." It is all very well to bring a piece of legislation before the House, to get it passed, and then to stand back and say that we have done our part. But, in the name of goodness, what is it doing to solve problems or to assist people when they need it? What is being done so that these people can survive, even possibly try to upgrade or keep up with the nurturing of their land? I would venture to say that across Canada today-and possibly many farmers could verify this-there are many hectares of farmland which are not being nurtured or have not received any type of fertilizer program. They are going an extra year without doing the fertilizing which they know should be done because they do not have the economics to carry it out. The country will suffer if the Government allows economics to interfere with the planning and development of our farming industry.
November 4, 1982

I urge the Government not to stop here. I urge Government Members to get out and visit farming areas across the land; they should meet with the farmers. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and his group should be visiting them to see first-hand and to ensure that there are provisions to meet their needs. Then we could start in that sector to ensure that the economy begins to work a little better.
Canada has one of the greatest agricultural potentials of any country in the world. We have the expertise. Farmers are proud of what they are doing. All we require is a government willing to give the lead and the confidence for farmers to carry on in a constructive and orderly way. They should not be faced with the roadblocks the Government seems to throw in front of them at every turn as soon as they start to improve something or to produce. I urge the Government to rethink some of its policies. It should look toward developing, helping and assisting farming communities right across the country.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON PRIVATE SECTOR
THE ECONOMY-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON PRIVATE SECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 1 in this House, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) a question referring to a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who said, "We haven't been able to make it work-the free enterprise system. We've ended up with very high unemployment and very high inflation. We can't go back to what it was before. That means the Government is going to take a larger role in running institutions." But the Minister of Finance in his economic address, his non-
Adjournment Debate
budget, states in the third of his six principles that we must continue to rely primarily on the dynamism and creativity of the private sector as the engine of growth in Canada. I think it is well known in this House that the Minister of Finance had agreed with that statement of the Prime Minister. Suddenly he declares six principles that go directly against what the Prime Minister had been speaking about. I would like to review some of these principles.
First, the Minister of Finance said that we must continue to practice fiscal responsibility and that we must persist in restraining Government spending. But what do we have? We have a deficit that has risen from $10.5 billion as indicated in last November's budget, to $19.6 billion in the June budget and to $23.6 billion in the non-budget of October. The thinking is that the deficit will be $26 billion before we are through.
Why should we believe what the Minister of Finance is telling us? Spending is up 17 per cent this year. The deficit is up $4 billion in four months-not $4 billion in one year, but $4 billion in four months. The Government will not even tell us what the deficit will be next year because it is afraid to admit what it will amount to. One dollar out of every three dollars in tax money goes to service the interest on the deficit. The interest on the national debt is $16.7 billion alone. This is a ridiculous situation. Why should we believe that the Minister of Finance has suddenly done a complete turn around and is no longer espousing his socialist ways?
Second, the Minister of Finance said that we must not abandon the victims of the recession in the mistaken belief that such callous action might speed our recovery. What a bunch of bunk. We have 12.2 per cent unemployment, yet the Minister of Finance stands in this House and tells us that. We have 1.4 million people out of work. We have 500,000 more people out of work than last year. This represents a tax loss of $2 billion. Yet we hear the Minister of Finance standing up and saying that we are going to turn the economy around.
The Minister also stands up and says that we are going to provide $500 million to help 60,000 people. What the Minister does not tell us is that this does not mean 60,000 jobs for a year. They may be jobs for one day simply to put an individual back on unemployment insurance. The jobs could last longer, but we do not know that. There are not 60,000 jobs allocated. That was never intended, but that is what the Minister of Finance would like us to believe. 1 come now to the Minister's fifth principle. He said that must continue to develop effective mechanisms for consultation with the provinces. We all remember the Kirby Report which the Minister of Finance approved. We all have that report. It described how the Government would divide the provinces when the Constitution was to be discussed. And this is the Finance Minister who wants us to believe him? And how long ago did this Prime Minister say that co-operative federalism is dead because he did not trust the provinces. Yet the Minister of Finance stood up and said that he had the method of recovery in this country.

November 4, 1982
Adjournment Debate
The sixth and most important point is that we must build on the spirit of the six and five program and implement an effective strategy for national recovery and economic development.
We all heard the Prime Minister a few weeks ago. In fact, one year ago we saw the geese flying across the television screen. A few weeks ago we had the lame duck flying across the television screen in the person of the Prime Minister. He said that Canadians should accept sacrifices. How many sacrifices is he accepting when every few weeks during the winter he flies down to the Caribbean to snorkle? He is not accepting any sacrifices.
Where was the Prime Minister in 1980 when we told him that the country was entering a recession? All he did was stand across the way and say that the Constitution is what we are interested in and what Canadians want. One million unemployed people later, he is still talking about it. We have seen no action from the Minister of Finance and no action from the Prime Minister.
The Minister of Finance tells us that we must adhere to the six and five program, but a few days before that program was announced he brought in a 10 per cent increase for the staff of all the Cabinet Ministers. They are not adhering to any program. The Government is giving us a high tax increase and a 40 per cent increase in UIC. About 500 CBC employees received an 11.5 per cent increase in wages. Where is the six and five program there? They are not adhering to the government program.
The real question is why we should believe anything the Minister of Finance says, or, for that matter, what his Parliamentary Secretary will say when he stands up.

Mr. Speaker, on occasion, we anticipate hearing from some speakers with some ideas, and that we will have to get out our hip waders just to survive. 1 have to say that the speech we have just heard is even worse than 1 had expected.
Today, we have a co-operative climate that exists between Government, business and labour; all working together to help rebuild the economy of this country. Let me give you some examples. The six and five program has been universally accepted by business, Government and ordinary people across this country. The $3,000 home mortgage grant has been universally accepted by the homebuilding industry. The 4 per cent interest reduction grants and the small business investment grants, along with the Small Business Bond have been widely accepted by Chambers of Commerce, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the Canadian Organization of Small Business. It is widely accepted that we should go out and put more money into the Farm Credit Corporation, and this was especially agreeable to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We have programs introduced by the June budget and the October statement which are productive sources of new jobs and new economic activity. The Hon. Member opposite has ignored all of these programs. In fact, the Hon. Member has followed a course of action that is currently typical of Tory tactics. He is creating fear and
loathing and using personal attacks to substitute for logic and tough debate. An example of that kind of activity is the Tory Party's attack in the past year on F1RA. They have attacked FIR A with unrelenting hatred, so much so that when their leader and their finance critic realized what they were unleashing, they had to make a 180 degree turn and start supporting the agency again. They became too hypocritical.
1 want to conclude by saying that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his speeches challenged us to attack our problems in the traditional Canadian way; through co-operation and working together. I would suggest to the Hon. Mr. Speaker, it was a very interesting exchange that we just witnessed. I will attempt to be reasonable in my submissions here this evening. 1 see the Parliamentary Secretary is leaving and I find that unfortunate because I had hoped he would stay and listen to some of my logic and tough debating skills with which I will make my case here this evening.
I had an opportunity in July, after having a discussion with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), and corresponding with him, to ask him a question in the House as to whether he would be prepared to raise the level of cash advances to prairie grain farmers. Cash advances are simply moneys advanced to prairie grain producers against their future sales. They are really advances against their own products-their own money.
The federal Government comes into play because it pays the interest on the money borrowed to pay the advances. The program was initiated for this back in 1957. It is a program which has worked very well. It has put money into farmers' pockets, enabling them to pay bills sooner than they would normally pay them if they had to wait for the sale of their products. This helped the whole community because it means that having cash in advance of their sales farmers are able to pay their taxes, repair bills, fuel bills, and those kinds of ordinary expenses incurred in the normal course of operating their farms.
We all know that the economic system is a circular one. What is an expense for one person then becomes income for someone else. As it goes through the system, that money is spent over and over again. If one wants to speak in economic terms, it is called the multiplier effect. If one looks at what goes on in the farming communities, and in other communities, one finds that farmers have a greater multiplying effect than those in most other industries. It simply means that when a dollar is put into a farmer's pocket, it is used more times. The program is essentially designed to put money into the hands of those in the farming community so that they can use it to pay
November 4, 1982

their bills, and this in turn provides income to other sectors of the economy.
As I have said, this has worked very well in the past. There have been very few defaults and very few problems in collecting money once it is advanced. However, the program is now sadly outdated in terms of the amount of money available. I will just give a couple of figures to illustrate.
In 1980 the number of applicants amounted to a few more than 15,000. The number of dollars advanced was in the order of $61 million. If we look at the figures for 1981, we find that the number of applicants almost doubled, rising from 15,000 to
28,000.	However, the amount of money advanced tripled, from $61 million to $205 million. This is an indicator, first of all, of not only how well received and well used the program is, but also an indicator that farmers were experiencing economic problems and needed some additional money to help pay some of their bills.
When the program was started in 1957, the cash advance limit was originally $5,000. It was increased once since then and is now set at $15,000. What we have suggested is that that limit be increased from $15,000 to $25,000, to $30,000 or to whatever figure is appropriate.
The cost to the federal treasury comes about because the Federal Government picks up the interest charges on the amount of money borrowed by the Canadian Wheat Board to make those cash advances. Admittedly, the federal Government will incur some additional costs, but let me point out to the Parliamentary Secretary that when that money is borrowed, it is borrowed by the Canadian Wheat Board on its behalf, and the Canadian Wheat Board, for the information of the Parliamentary Secretary and those who are interested, borrows money at the prime rate minus a quarter of one per cent. I know of no one else in this country who borrows money at the prime rate minus any figure. Therefore, because of the favourable financial position of the Wheat Board, it is able to borrow money more cheaply than the Government and more cheaply than producers. That is a good, healthy, sound reason why, by increasing those levels of cash advances, the extra interest will not hurt the federal Government as much as one might suppose.
Aside from that fact, I would submit that the additional cost is well worth it because in hard economic times that money is not hoarded by farmers but, rather, is spent and respent, creating additional economic activity, which is what we are attempting to do by Bill C-134, which we just finished discussing this evening. It is designed to help farmers meet some of their financial commitments. That is precisely what increasing the level of cash advances would do.
I have received letters from several farm organizations across the prairies, as I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary has, suggesting that the limit be raised from $10,000 to $50,000. I suspect that is probably too much to ask, but the Government could surely consider increasing the limit from $15,000 to $25,000. After all, in the same period of time, the Government has increased the levy against producers who are in the Western Grains Stabilization Fund. The amount has been doubled. It has gone from a maximum of $500 to $900
Adjournment Debate
this year and it is about to go up to $1,200, so it has more than doubled in the period of time that the cash advance program has remained the same.
As spokesman on the Canadian Wheat Board for this Party I offered the Minister of Transport an arrangement whereby we would very quickly pass the amendment that would be required to the Act. We would not hold up debate and would not put up a lot of speakers so that it could go through very quickly. This matter was considered to be very urgent last year, on July 30, when I first posed the question. That was before the start of the new crop year. It is equally urgent now, because farmers are facing a very tough winter. Although the additional cash advances would not be totally utilized this year as a lot of farmers have already delivered grain, against which those cash advances would have to be deducted, the program would still be well received. As I have pointed out, the Program has been very well run in the past. Losses have been minimal.
1 hope the Parliamentary Secretary will take these things into consideration and will make the positive announcement tonight that the Government has considered our offer. I hope he will be able to tell us when it is prepared to bring the legislation forward. We will not hold it up, Mr. Speaker. In that way we will be able to increase the level of cash advances and in this way not only the Canadian farmer but the whole Canadian economy will benefit.

subtopic: GRAIN-LEVELS OF ADVANCE PAYMENTS. (B) POSSIBLE BENEFITS TO WESTERN COMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's interest in this subject is well-known in the House. I applaud him for making a reasonable case on behalf of the western farmer. As one who was born, raised and lived for 18 years on a farm in Saskatchewan, I know how tough it is to find the cash in advance for the purchase of new machinery, to put in crops and even to buy groceries. I appreciate the co-operative spirit in which the Hon. Member presented his argument-unlike the previous speaker. I thank him for that.
It is very clear that farmers are making good use of the opportunities available under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. The number of producers who qualify for the maximum advance of $15,000 is increasing, as the Hon. Member pointed out tonight. Therefore, it is reasonable to suggest that the maximum be increased, especially at a time when farmers are experiencing higher cash requirements. As the Minister said in his answer on July 30, this question was considered by his colleagues and a decision was deferred until the question could be put in "the wider context of western grain initiatives".
One of the factors which must clearly be advanced in times of restraint, is the cost. In 1981-82, the cost was $12.7 million. The Hon. Member suggested that the advance payments should be increased to $25,000 or $30,000. My calculations show that the resulting cost would probably be over $25

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION-DELAY IN APPOINTING CANADIAN COMMISSIONER
INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION-DELAY IN APPOINTING CANADIAN COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly about the International Joint Commission and the serious problems it is confronting. The studies of the Commission are crucial to the people of my riding in Erie which is located in the heart of the Great Lakes basin. Although much work has been done and much concern expressed, the health and well-being of my constituents and Canadians continues to be threatened by chemical pollution in Lake Erie, Lake Ontario and the Niagara and St. Clair Rivers.
The stated purpose of the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement of 1978 is "to restore and maintain the chemical, physical and biological integrity of the waters of the Great Lakes basin ecosystem." This is indeed an ambitious statement. To comprehend the vast extent of the problem confronting the commission, it is only necessary to look at the following statistics.
The Great Lakes Basin is a highly developed industrial and agricultural region. The present population of 37 million people should increase to 60 million by the year 2020. This increased urban growth will engender accompanying industrial development. Both of these phenomena mean that there will be vastly increased stresses on all the components of the ecosystem.
Not only are the Great Lakes presently being overloaded with garbage at a rate much more than they can handle right now, but the amount of effluent both from industrial and human sources is expected to greatly increase in the new few years. This in itself would be serious enough for the Government of one country to deal with. But here we have two countries, both of which have different priorities and different policies. The need for co-operation and compromise has never been greater, in order to come to agreement on protective and preventative measures which are satisfactory to both parties.
Currently in the Great Lakes Basin, approximately 800 major municipal and industrial facilities are dumping hazardous wastes into the Great Lakes. Smaller contributors number in the thousands. With input of toxic chemicals, phosphorous residues from detergents and fertilizers and superficially treated inflow from municipal sewage treatment plants, it is unlikely that the original state of the Great Lakes can ever be restored.
However, a continued degradation of Great Lakes water quality cannot be tolerated. Reasonable objectives are attainable nevertheless. These include reversal of the over-all longterm trend of water pollution, enabling inhabitants of the area to drink clean water, swim without danger of contamination and to enjoy the recreational resources of the lakes, including fishing and boating. The Boundary Waters Treaty states that those waters whose shoreline or banks are shared by the two countries shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other.
I am concerned, as a representative in Ottawa of a constituency bordering on one of the Great Lakes that little action is being taken to be sure that both parties adhere to the terms of the treaty. Certain areas have been, and continue to be identified by the commission as being environmental or human health concerns.
In looking at the August 1982 report of the International Joint Commission, I note that there are 24 different areas which have been identified as "problem areas". In many of these areas, especially the Niagara and St. Clair Rivers, much more work needs to be done. As stated in the report, "there is little value in continuing to identify such areas if effective remedial efforts are not put into place".
The environmental baseline report of the Niagara River of November 1981 states that the Niagara River has been identified as the major source of numerous trace metals and organic compounds to Lake Ontario. Less than 1 per cent of the loadings of these substances to the river can be accounted for from Canadian sources. The Niagara River is a primary source of the PCBs and the Mirex which have been found in fish and in herring gulls throughout Lake Ontario.
Obviously in this case we, the Canadians, are the ones being injured by pollution from American sources. This situation of course, can no longer be tolerated. Such sources of pollution as the Hooker Chemical Corporation and the municipal wastewater treatment plant in Niagara Falls, New York, pour volumes of pollutants into the river equal to or greater than the total amount coming from Canadian sources.
Given the inequity of this situation we, as concerned representatives of the people of this land, must do everything in our power to convince the Reagan administration that this issue must be dealth with in a firm and conclusive manner before it is too late. Only by co-operation with the United States can this problem be solved. Given the small percentage of the total load of chemicals emanating from Canada, unilateral action on our part seems almost ridiculous-not that our own industries are entirely innocent. I am sure there exists blatant examples of environmental misconduct among Canadian companies as well.
In summary, it is time to stop talking and begin acting. There are just too many 40-page descriptions of the callous destruction of our most valuable heritage, the Great Lakes. We need 40-page solutions outlining in detail the method of ameliorating this unfortunate situation in order that our descendants may enjoy the same fresh, clear, safe waters that our ancestors enjoyed.
November 4, 1982
